| Show Base64 offsets | redesigned | `base64-offsets:show` | Text, not HTML. With show-variable on (the default, as CyberChef's Show variable chars and padding) three lines Offset 0: ..., Offset 1: ..., Offset 2: ... hold the Base64 of the data behind 0, 1 and 2 zero bytes, in full, including the leading characters that stand for the unknown bytes and the padding, as CyberChef writes them (it colours them; text cannot, so nothing marks them). With it off the three lines have no label and hold only the static characters. CyberChef also writes four lines of colour legend above the offsets and shows the decoded static part as a tooltip; text has neither. Written in FL over the base64 primitive and a 256-byte translation table. Parameters as CyberChef: alphabet (ranges such as A-Za-z0-9+/=, 64 or 65 characters), show variable chars and padding, input format (raw, base64 and, as an addition, hex). Added checks: the alphabet must be 64 or 65 different ASCII characters (E_RANGE), invalid hex or Base64 input is E_COERCE; empty input is E_COERCE as CyberChef's error. | AMF Encode | redesigned | `amf:encode` | JSON text to one AMF0 or AMF3 value (Adobe's specifications), by a private writer primitive. Parameter format AMF0 or AMF3 (the default is AMF3, as CyberChef's). AMF0: every number as a double, text as a string (long string above 65535 bytes), arrays as strict arrays, objects as anonymous objects, null as null. AMF3: integers from -2^28 to 2^28-1 as AMF3 integers, other numbers as doubles, text as a string, arrays as dense arrays, objects as dynamic anonymous objects. No reference tables are written, byte arrays, dates and typed objects cannot be written (JSON has no such values), an empty property name and nesting deeper than 64 levels are E_COERCE. Vectors built by hand from the specifications and checked against the amfy library. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read and the library @astronautlabs/amf 0.0.6 run. The bytes are not the same and are not meant to be: the library writes every AMF3 number as a double and objects as sealed traits, fails on non-ASCII property names and on arrays in AMF3, keeps state between calls (a later AMF0 encode of {} returned the bytes of earlier objects) and counts the AMF0 long-string limit in characters. Forge writes AMF3 integers where they fit, dynamic objects and correct lengths. Every AMF3 value the library wrote and that was not damaged by those faults decodes to the same JSON with amf:decode (192 of 212 values; the rest are the library's state leaks). |

String, object and trait references are followed and the shared values copied under the value budget (a reference to an object still being read, a cycle, is E_COERCE because JSON cannot show it); the AMF0 avmplus marker switches to AMF3. Compared with the jsrsasign dump by running CyberChef on a certificate: differences are INTEGER shown in full (CyberChef truncates), BIT STRING and OCTET STRING without the word 'encapsulates', ENUMERATED in hex, OID names from Forge's table, and truncate counts bytes (CyberChef shows that many hex characters from each end). Not aligned in this pass. Text, not a record tree, because the output pane shows trees only 6 levels deep and a certificate nests deeper once its extension values are opened; the record tree is the shared word asn1:parse, for FL code. Parameters: start (a byte offset; CyberChef counts hex characters and then shows the first element only, here every element from there to the end is shown) and truncate (bytes of a value to show, default 32 as in CyberChef; 0 shows all). Malformed data (cut short, indefinite length, nesting over 64 levels, trailing bytes that are not an element) is E_COERCE, where CyberChef prints what it could read. | CSV to JSON | redesigned | `csv:to-json` | RFC 4180 reading by a private scanner primitive; the rows-to-JSON mapping is FL over the shared json words. Parameters as CyberChef: cell delimiter (default ","), row delimiter (default \r\n) and format (array of dictionaries, the default, or array of arrays). Each delimiter is a set of characters, any one of which ends a cell or a row, so the default row delimiter reads CRLF, LF and CR; both are read for the escapes \r \n \t \\ and \xHH so they can be typed in a text box. Every value is a JSON string. A cell that starts with a double quote runs to the closing quote and may hold delimiters and line breaks, a doubled quote is one quote, and a quote inside an unquoted cell is kept. Deliberate strictness, each an error rather than a silent repair: an unterminated quote or text after a closing quote is E_COERCE with the offset, line and column; in the dictionaries format a row whose cell count differs from the header, or a repeated header name, is E_COERCE (nothing is dropped or overwritten); the delimiters must be non-empty, must not be the double quote and must not share a character (E_RANGE). Empty lines are skipped. An added indent parameter (default 4 spaces, as CyberChef's JSON output; 0 for compact text) saves a chain step. A byte order mark at the start is dropped, as CyberChef does. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source of the operation and Utils.parseCSV read, and the delimiters, defaults and the dictionary and array layouts are CyberChef's. Remaining differences: CyberChef toggles quoting at any double quote, also inside an unquoted cell, and drops a last row that has no row end after its first cell (a last line 'c' is lost when the earlier lines were rows); it fills missing cells with undefined and drops extra cells; Forge keeps RFC 4180 reading and raises the errors above. |
| JSON to CSV | redesigned | `csv:from-json` | JSON text parsed strictly by the shared json:parse and written as RFC 4180 CSV by a private writer primitive. Parameters as CyberChef: cell delimiter (default ",") and row delimiter (default \r\n; the escapes \r \n \t \\ and \xHH are read). The input is an array of objects (a header row of the keys, then a row each), an array of arrays (rows only) or one object (a header and one row); every row, the last one too, is followed by the row delimiter (CyberChef's layout). The header holds the keys of all the objects in order of first appearance, with an empty cell where an object has no key (CyberChef takes the keys of the first object only and writes undefined for a key an object lacks). Strings are written as they are, null as an empty cell (CyberChef writes the word null), and numbers, true, false, arrays and objects as their JSON text (big integers exact; CyberChef flattens nested values to a.b keys instead). A cell is quoted when it holds the cell delimiter, the row delimiter, a double quote, a CR or an LF, and a row of one empty cell is written "" so it is not a blank line. Deliberate strictness: an array that mixes objects and arrays or holds other values, a repeated key (JSON text is parsed, so the duplicate is E_COERCE), malformed JSON and a top-level scalar are E_COERCE. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read, and the cell quoting rule, the default delimiters and the trailing row delimiter are CyberChef's. An empty array is empty text here and an error there. |

| YAML to JSON | redesigned | `yaml:to-json` | The reader is the yaml library (ISC), not js-yaml, and reads the YAML 1.2 core schema; CyberChef 11.5.0's js-yaml 5 reads the YAML 1.2 core schema too (run: yes and 2001-01-01 are strings, 0x1f an integer), and fails on !!binary and !!set where Forge keeps their text. Here null, ~ and an empty value are null, true and false are the only booleans, integers (decimal, 0x, 0o) are exact with big integers kept, merge keys work, and a timestamp, !!binary, !!set or any other tag is not interpreted (the text stays a string). Like js-yaml: more than one document and a repeated key are errors. Stricter by design, each an E_COERCE with the offset, line and column or the reason: .inf and .nan (CyberChef writes null), a mapping key that is a collection, two keys that become the same text, an alias to a collection that contains it, a lone surrogate. Bounds: aliases are shared references and the expansion is charged to the value limit while the value is built (a billion-laughs document is E_LIMIT_VALUE), nesting deeper than 512 levels is E_LIMIT_VALUE. JSON output is indented by 4 spaces as CyberChef writes it; an added indent parameter (0 to 32, 0 is compact) saves a chain step. Floats print as the other JSON words print them (1.0, 1e+21). An empty stream is null. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): js-yaml 5.4.1 run on the same documents: the JSON agrees except for the differences listed (more than one document is an error in both; .inf is null there and an error here). |
| JSON to YAML | redesigned | `yaml:from-json` | Written by the yaml library in the layout of js-yaml's dump defaults (block style, 2-space indent, single quotes, keys in the order of the JSON text), reading the JSON with the shared strict parser. Differences from js-yaml, all cosmetic or safer: a long string is folded as a multi-line plain scalar instead of >-; a float with no fraction keeps it (1.0 is written 1.0, so the reader sees a float again); strings that YAML 1.1 or 1.2 would read as another type are quoted, as is a string with a tab or the strings << and =; a big integer is written exactly. A repeated key, a lone surrogate or malformed JSON is E_COERCE. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): js-yaml 5.4.1 run on four JSON values (objects, nested lists, multi-line and special strings, floats): the YAML text is identical. |
| Caret/M-decode | covered | `caret:decode` | The inverse of cat -v; caret:encode is the matching encoder. |
| Rison Encode | redesigned | `rison:encode` | JSON text to Rison, O-Rison or A-Rison by a private writer primitive: one op with a mode parameter (rison, o-rison, a-rison, uri) for CyberChef's Encode, Encode Object, Encode Array and Encode URI. Rules of rison.js: !t !f !n, !(a,b) arrays, (k:v) objects with sorted keys (by UTF-16 code unit), bare identifiers or single-quoted strings with ' and ! escaped by !, numbers as JavaScript prints them without the + (an integer in full digits, so 1.0 is 1). O-Rison of a non-object and A-Rison of a non-array are E_COERCE; nesting deeper than 64 levels is E_COERCE. Vectors from Python prison and the rison.js rules (numbers derived by hand). Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): read the source and ran the libraries CyberChef 11.5.0 uses (cbor2 2.3.0, notepack.io, avsc, @astronautlabs/amf 0.0.6, rison 0.1.1): the output of all four modes agrees with rison.js on 18 values, 72 cases. Encode URI quotes the text as rison.quote does (encodeURIComponent but ~!*()-_.',:@$/ stay, space is +); rison.js 0.1.1 passes a third argument to String.replace that modern engines ignore, so it restores only the first of each of , : @ $ / in a text that needs quoting; Forge restores all (the vectors use Python's quote_plus). |
| Rison Decode | redesigned | `rison:decode` | Rison, O-Rison and A-Rison text to JSON text by a private reader primitive, mode parameter as in the encoder. White space is allowed around the text only; integers without fraction or exponent are exact, a repeated key, a bad number, an unknown ! form, an unterminated string or list, text after the value and nesting deeper than 64 levels are E_COERCE with the offset. Added parameter indent (default 4). Vectors from Python prison. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read; the modes are CyberChef's Decode, Decode Object and Decode Array, with the JSON indent of 4. |
| To Modhex | covered | `modhex:encode` |  |
| From Modhex | covered | `modhex:decode` |  |
| MIME Decoding | covered | `mime:decode` | Written in FL over the regex words, base64 and charset. The encoded-word of RFC 2047 in B or Q form is decoded in any character set the charset vocabulary knows by its MIME name (CyberChef: utf-8, us-ascii, iso-8859-1 to 16); white space between two words is dropped, a language part (utf-8*en) is ignored, CRLF is read as LF as CyberChef does. A word must be well formed (no white space or ? inside) to be decoded, otherwise it stays as text; an unknown character set, bad base64, bad =XX or invalid bytes are E_COERCE. iso-8859-9, -11 and -12 are not offered (the charset vocabulary has no true table for them). CyberChef's charsets are those of the codepage library; the words of one set are decoded in a single call of the decoder (WP 5.59c: a header of thousands of encoded words in a set other than UTF-8, ISO-8859-1 and ASCII no longer reaches the total allocation limit, which came at about 1,800 words). Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read; the white space rule, the Q and B decoding and the CRLF reading are CyberChef's. CyberChef's decoder keeps a failed word's text and throws Unhandled Charset for an unknown set; the errors here are E_COERCE. |

| AES Encrypt | redesigned | `aes:encrypt` | Bytes in and bytes out (CyberChef's Input and Output encodings are chain steps such as hex:decode and hex:encode). The key and the IV are key params in any of the key encodings, the key 16, 24 or 32 bytes. The mode is CBC (the default), CFB, OFB, CTR, GCM or ECB, and padding is its own choice (pkcs7, the default, or none), where CyberChef has separate CBC/NoPadding and ECB/NoPadding modes. GCM takes the additional data as the aad param and appends the 16-byte tag to the ciphertext, where CyberChef returns the tag separately. A wrong key or IV length is E_RANGE. CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. GCM needs an IV of at least 8 bytes (E_RANGE otherwise; CyberChef accepts any length, even none, which the library behind Forge does not). An empty IV is E_RANGE in CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR as in CyberChef. CyberChef's Include IV in output (Off, Prepend, Append) is a chain step: cat the IV in front of or behind the output. |
| AES Decrypt | redesigned | `aes:decrypt` | The inverse of aes:encrypt with the same parameters. For GCM the last 16 bytes of the input are the tag (CyberChef takes a separate GCM Tag param), and a tag that does not verify is E_COERCE and returns no plaintext; bad PKCS#7 padding is E_COERCE too. The no-padding modes of CyberChef are padding none. CyberChef's IV from input (From start or From end) is a chain step: slice the IV off the input and pass it as the iv param. CTR counts as in aes:encrypt (the last four bytes). |

CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. |
| Blowfish Decrypt | redesigned | `blowfish:decrypt` | The inverse of blowfish:encrypt with the same parameters. |

CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. |

CTR adds one to the last four bytes of the counter block only, modulo 2^32 with no carry into the rest, as CyberChef does (node-forge's inc32); a whole-block counter (the usual reading of SP 800-38A) gives the same key stream until the low word wraps, after 2^32 blocks. |
| Triple DES Decrypt | redesigned | `triple-des:decrypt` | The inverse of triple-des:encrypt with the same parameters. |
| Fernet Encrypt | redesigned | `fernet:encrypt` | Fernet (github.com/fernet/spec) in FL over aes:encrypt, hmac:digest and base64: version 0x80, an 8-byte time, a 16-byte IV, AES-128-CBC with PKCS#7, HMAC-SHA256, url-safe base64 with padding. The input is bytes and the token is its text as bytes. The key is a key param: 32 bytes, or their url-safe base64 text (the form CyberChef takes; 43 or 44 characters), anything else E_RANGE. The IV comes from the host CSPRNG (the +random effect) and the time from the clock (+time), as in CyberChef, so the output differs on every call; nothing falls back to Math.random (a host with no crypto.getRandomValues is E_PRIMITIVE). Tests pin both through the private fernet:_seal. |

The key is the same key param as in fernet:encrypt. CyberChef fixes the TTL at 0 (no time check); an added ttl param (seconds, default 0 = no check) applies the spec's age rules: older than the TTL, or more than 60 seconds in the future, is E_COERCE. The base64 padding is optional on input. |

CyberChef runs CBC when an IV is given and ECB when it is blank, with no other setting; here mode (CBC, the default, or ECB) is explicit, so a blank IV in CBC is E_RANGE. The RFC's effective key bits are the effective-bits param (1 to 1024), whose default 128 is what CyberChef's library uses for any key length. Key 1 to 128 bytes; padding is its own choice. Effective bits that are not a multiple of 8 follow RFC 2268 (the vectors cover 63 and 129); the library behind CyberChef masks those wrongly, but CyberChef never sets them. |

| RC4 Drop | redesigned | `rc4:crypt` | The same word as RC4 with the drop param, counted in bytes where CyberChef counts dwords: CyberChef's default of 192 dwords is drop 768. One word covers both rows because RC4-drop is RC4 with the first n key stream bytes discarded. |
| ChaCha | redesigned | `chacha:encrypt` | One word, encrypt, for both directions (a stream cipher), with the key and the nonce as key params in any of the four encodings (the Integer nonce toggle is not offered), the block counter as a number from 0, and rounds as a choice of 20, 12 or 8. The layouts follow noble: a 12-byte nonce with a 4-byte counter (RFC 8439) takes a 32-byte key and 20, 12 or 8 rounds; an 8-byte nonce with an 8-byte counter takes a 16- or 32-byte key and 20 rounds only. A 16-byte key with a 12-byte nonce, which CyberChef accepts, is E_RANGE, because noble has no such core and none is written here. A counter that would overflow is E_RANGE (noble refuses it), where CyberChef truncates. Input and output are bytes (chain hex:decode and hex:encode for text). The counter is limited to 32 bits for both layouts (noble's counter; the 8-byte nonce layout has a 64-bit counter in CyberChef): a counter or a message that would take it past 2^32 - 1 is E_RANGE. Rounds 12 and 8 are available for the 12-byte nonce only. For every combination that is offered the key stream equals CyberChef's. |
| Salsa20 | redesigned | `salsa20:encrypt` | One word, encrypt, for both directions, with the key (16 or 32 bytes), the 8-byte nonce and the block counter as CyberChef has them, except that the counter is limited to 32 bits (noble's), so one that would pass 2^32 - 1 is E_RANGE where CyberChef has a 64-bit counter. There is no rounds parameter: noble runs Salsa20/20 only, so CyberChef's 12 and 8 rounds are not offered (no own core is written for them). The Integer nonce toggle is not offered. A counter that would overflow is E_RANGE. |
| XSalsa20 | redesigned | `xsalsa20:encrypt` | One word, encrypt, for both directions, with the 24-byte nonce and the block counter as CyberChef has them, except that the counter is limited to 32 bits (noble's), so one that would pass 2^32 - 1 is E_RANGE where CyberChef has a 64-bit counter. The key is 32 bytes only: noble has no 16-byte XSalsa20, so CyberChef's 16-byte key is E_RANGE. There is no rounds parameter (20 rounds only, as for Salsa20), and no Integer nonce toggle (an 8-byte integer nonce is not a valid XSalsa20 nonce). |

| SM4 Encrypt | redesigned | `sm4:encrypt` | GB/T 32907-2016, 16-byte key and IV, modes CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB. CyberChef's CBC/NoPadding and ECB/NoPadding modes are padding none. An empty input encrypts to one block of padding in CBC and ECB where CyberChef returns nothing. |

| RC6 Encrypt | redesigned | `rc6:encrypt` | RC6-w/r with CyberChef's parameters: word-size (a multiple of 8, 8 to 256, default 32) and rounds (1 to 255, default 20); an empty IV is zero bytes as in CyberChef; modes CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and ECB. Padding is pkcs7 or none: CyberChef's ZERO, RANDOM and BIT paddings are not offered (the shared padding is PKCS#7), and empty input encrypts to one padding block where CyberChef returns nothing. Word sizes other than 32 use BigInt arithmetic and are slow. CTR reads the counter block as a little-endian integer (the first byte is the least significant) and adds one per block, as CyberChef's RC6 does, so it differs from the big-endian counter of the other ciphers after the first block. The block is w / 2 bytes, so word-size 8 has 4-byte blocks (the modes work for any block size). |

Only the HMAC algorithms HS256, HS384 and HS512 are offered; CyberChef's RS, ES and PS algorithms are public-key and belong to wave 7, and None (an unsigned token) is deliberately not offered. The key is a key param (not empty, else E_RANGE). The input is the payload JSON text and is signed exactly as given (it is not parsed or re-serialised, because FL has no JSON parser; it must be a JSON object by its first and last character, else E_COERCE). The header is {"alg":...,"typ":"JWT"} followed by the members of the header param (a JSON object text; typ there replaces the default, alg there is E_RANGE), where CyberChef merges a parsed object. CyberChef's library (jsonwebtoken) parses the payload, adds an iat (issued at) claim when there is none and signs the re-serialised JSON; here the text is signed exactly as given and nothing is added, so a payload that already holds an iat and is compact JSON signs to the same token. |
| JWT Verify | redesigned | `jwt:verify` | Verifies HS256, HS384 and HS512 under the key and returns the payload as the JSON text the token holds, as CyberChef returns the payload (a failure raises E_COERCE, there is no bool). The alg param is auto (the token's own header chooses among the three HMAC algorithms, which is safe because only a shared secret is accepted) or a pinned algorithm. alg none is never accepted, whatever the key or pin (E_RANGE), and neither is any algorithm that is not HS256/384/512 (RS, ES and PS are wave 7: E_RANGE). A header with the text "alg" twice is ambiguous (E_COERCE). Unlike CyberChef (jsonwebtoken) the exp and nbf claims are not checked: this is a signature check, because that needs a JSON parser and a clock. |
| JWT Decode | redesigned | `jwt:decode` | Splits a compact token and decodes the payload (or, with the part param, the header), without a key, as the JSON text the token holds, exactly as written (CyberChef returns the parsed payload). Each decoded part must be a JSON object by its first and last character, and the token three parts (an encrypted five-part JWT is E_COERCE); the JSON is not parsed further because FL has no JSON parser. |
| Citrix CTX1 Encode | covered | `classical:ctx1-encode` |  |
| Citrix CTX1 Decode | covered | `classical:ctx1-decode` |  |
| AES Key Wrap | redesigned | `aes-kw:wrap` | RFC 3394 over noble's aeskw, with the key-encryption key (16, 24 or 32 bytes, a key-type param) and the input as bytes. The IV is the RFC 3394 default, A6A6A6A6A6A6A6A6, fixed by noble, so CyberChef's IV parameter is not offered (a custom IV is not RFC 3394's algorithm as noble implements it). The input must be a multiple of 8 bytes and at least 16 (E_COERCE otherwise, as CyberChef). RFC 5649 padding is not offered, because CyberChef does not offer it. The output is raw bytes (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's Hex output). |
| AES Key Unwrap | redesigned | `aes-kw:unwrap` | The inverse of aes-kw:wrap under the same key-encryption key, with the same IV and no IV or padding parameters for the reason given for AES Key Wrap. The wrapped key must be a multiple of 8 bytes and at least 24 (E_COERCE otherwise). A wrong key or corrupted data fails the RFC 3394 integrity check: E_COERCE, and no key data is returned (CyberChef reports an IV mismatch error). |
| Pseudo-Random Number Generator | redesigned | `prng:bytes` | Bytes out: a number of random bytes (32 by default, 0 to 1 MiB) from the host CSPRNG (crypto.getRandomValues, never Math.random). CyberChef's Hex (its default), Integer, Byte array and Raw output menu is a chain step (hex:encode, base64:encode, and so on). Like CyberChef the input is ignored. A host with no random source is E_PRIMITIVE. |
| Pseudo-Random Prime Generator | redesigned | `prime:generate` | A prime drawn uniformly from the primes of exactly size bits (2 to 2048; 512 by default, as CyberChef's bit length) or size decimal digits (1 to 616) by rejection sampling on the host CSPRNG (crypto.getRandomValues, never Math.random), tested by trial division and Miller-Rabin with random bases (40 rounds below 256 bits, 8 above). Several primes can be asked for (count, up to 100, joined by a delimiter of the wave 5 list), as decimal text or lower-case hex text with 0x in front, as CyberChef writes it. CyberChef draws a number below 2^bits, so its primes can be shorter; Forge's have exactly the size asked for. The input is ignored. A 2048-bit prime takes about two seconds. CyberChef's Crypto grade switch is not offered. |

It searches all 17,576 start positions with a crib at an offset, using the menu, the diagonal board and the test register, and lists the stops with the steckers deduced and a decryption preview made with enigma:encrypt. Enigma I and M3 only (no M4); stops are window letters at the start of the message. |
| Multiple Bombe | redesigned | `bombe:search` | The same word: give more than three rotors (up to five, 60 orders) and every order of three of them is searched, left rotor first; the output names the rotor order of each stop. Capped by rotor orders times menu edges so that a run finishes inside a bake. |
| Typex | redesigned | `typex:encrypt` | Real Typex rotor wirings were never published, so there is no built-in rotor set: the five rotor wirings, reflector, notches and reversed rotors are parameters (validated permutations of A-Z), with clearly labelled non-historical example defaults. The conventions (rotors written left to right with the signal entering at the right, notch letters tested after the step, reversed rotors as neg o inverse o neg, the entry plugboard as a 26-letter wiring entering c as -P(c), Enigma-style stepping with the double step) follow CyberChef's for compatibility; the real Typex conventions are unpublished. |
| Lorenz | redesigned | `lorenz:encrypt`, `lorenz:decrypt` | Two words with one set of parameters (model SZ40, SZ42a or SZ42b, the P5 attachment, KH, ZMUG, BREAM or custom wheel patterns, twelve start positions, text or ITA2 in and out); decrypt exists because the P5 limitation makes the key depend on the plain text. |
| Colossus | redesigned | `colossus:count` | A counting run over the start positions of two chi wheels with a Boolean condition on delta Z and delta chi (the 1+2 break-in by default), a set total and a table of the best settings; it does not model the plug panels and the tape reader of the machine, and it does not search three wheels at once. |
| SIGABA | covered | `sigaba:crypt` | One word with a mode parameter (encrypt or decrypt), the rotor choice, orientation (R suffix) and start positions of the three banks, and optional rotor wirings; the default wirings are Forge's own, not the historical ones. The index rotor offset (+d for digit d) follows CyberChef's convention for compatibility; the sources do not fix it. |
| Flask Session Decode | redesigned | `flask-session:decode` | itsdangerous's URLSafeTimedSerializer as Flask uses it, in FL over base64. Decodes the payload.timestamp.signature cookie to the session JSON text as written (not parsed). The View TimeStamp option is the timestamp param (default false); with it the result is {"payload":...,"timestamp":N}. The timestamp is read as itsdangerous writes it, the shortest big-endian integer, where CyberChef reads exactly 4 bytes. A cookie whose payload Flask compressed with zlib (it starts with a dot) is inflated with deflate:zlib-inflate, within the value limit (CyberChef cannot read these); a corrupt zlib stream is E_COERCE. CyberChef cannot decode a cookie with non-ASCII text (it fails), which is read here as UTF-8. |
| Flask Session Sign | redesigned | `flask-session:sign` | Signs a session JSON as a Flask cookie: salt cookie-session by default, the 'hmac' key derivation HMAC(secret, salt), a SHA-1 (default) or SHA-256 signature over payload.timestamp, url-safe base64 without padding. The key and the salt are key params (CyberChef's toggle encodings, minus Decimal and Binary which are chain steps); an empty key is E_RANGE (Secret key required) and an empty salt means the default, as CyberChef. The input JSON text is used as given. The time is the clock (the +time effect) unless the added timestamp param pins it (Unix seconds above 0; 0 is now), which also makes the word reproducible. Never compresses. CyberChef signs the re-serialised JSON, written as Latin-1 (it keeps the low byte of each character, so non-ASCII text comes out wrong); here the text is signed as given in UTF-8. For ASCII compact JSON the cookie equals CyberChef's. |
| Flask Session Verify | redesigned | `flask-session:verify` | Checks the signature as flask-session:sign writes it (E_COERCE when it does not verify, as CyberChef's Invalid signature) and returns {"valid":true,"payload":...} with ,"timestamp":N when the timestamp param is set (default true), as text rather than a parsed object. Same key, salt and algorithm params as flask-session:sign. A compressed (leading dot) payload is inflated, and the signature is checked over the dot as Flask signs it. The age of the cookie is not checked, as in CyberChef. |

The signature is deterministic (RFC 6979, which two independent implementations agree on); CyberChef's jsrsasign uses a random k, so the same key and message give a different signature there on every call and the same one here. Every ECDSA verifier accepts both. The input bytes are hashed as bytes (CyberChef decodes them as UTF-8 text first). raw-json writes r and s as the hex of their DER INTEGER content, as jsrsasign does (with a leading 00 when the top bit is set). Forge's sets hold each item once; CyberChef's symmetric difference keeps the repeats of an item inside one set (a,a,b against c is a,a,b,c there). |

Items are exact text and a set holds each item once, in order of first appearance. Exactly two sets (anything else is E_RANGE). Each pair is written (a,b) and the pairs are joined by the item delimiter, those of the first item of A first. Forge's sets hold each item once, so a repeated item makes no repeated pairs (CyberChef repeats them), and an empty set gives an empty product (CyberChef reads it as one empty item and writes (a,)). |
| Power Set | covered | `set:power-set` | One set cut at the item delimiter (a comma by default), without empty items; the subsets are written as their items joined by the item delimiter, each followed by the subset delimiter (a line feed by default, a Forge parameter), so the result starts with an empty line for the empty subset and ends with the delimiter, as CyberChef's does. The order is CyberChef's: binary counting with the first item as the most significant bit, then a stable sort by the length of the written subset. Duplicate items are removed first (CyberChef repeats the subsets they make). At most 16 distinct items (E_RANGE beyond), since the output has 2^n subsets. |

Where CyberChef silently ignores a piece that is not a number (and reads 0xff as hexadecimal), Forge raises E_COERCE naming it; no numbers at all is E_RANGE where CyberChef prints NaN. The arithmetic is exact decimal, as BigNumber's. The result is plain decimal text with no trailing zeros. |

The numbers are cut at a delimiter from the wave 5 list (a line feed by default, as in CyberChef; Forge adds cr and tab), blanks around a number and blank pieces are skipped. Where CyberChef silently ignores a piece that is not a number (and reads 0xff as hexadecimal), Forge raises E_COERCE naming it; no numbers at all is E_RANGE where CyberChef prints NaN. The arithmetic is exact decimal, as BigNumber's. |

The remainder has the sign of the dividend, like BigNumber's default, and is exact for decimals. The modulus is a text parameter, so it can be any decimal. A zero modulus is E_DIV_ZERO. The numbers are cut at a delimiter from the wave 5 list (a line feed by default, as in CyberChef; Forge adds cr and tab), blanks around a number and blank pieces are skipped. Where CyberChef silently ignores a piece that is not a number (and reads 0xff as hexadecimal), Forge raises E_COERCE naming it; no numbers at all is E_RANGE where CyberChef prints NaN. The output is CyberChef's report: gcd: g, a blank line, Bezout coefficients:, the lines x = and y =, each ending in a line feed. The coefficients are those of the iterative algorithm on the absolute values with the signs put back, so a * x + b * y = g holds also for a negative a or b; CyberChef's coefficients are the same for a and b of 0 or more, but they do not satisfy the identity when b is negative. g is never negative. Not an integer is E_COERCE. |

A negative exponent or a modulus below 1 is E_RANGE (CyberChef's negative exponent gives a wrong result, its modulus must be above zero); not an integer is E_COERCE. |

## Networking (34)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HTTP request | dropped |  | It sends a request to another host. The bake Web Worker runs under a CSP of connect-src 'self' and Forge never talks to another host (as for Show on map), so the operation cannot exist; use curl or a browser, and paste the response into Forge. |
| DNS over HTTPS | dropped |  | It asks a DNS-over-HTTPS resolver (Cloudflare or Google) over the network. The bake Web Worker's CSP is connect-src 'self' and Forge never talks to another host (as for Show on map), so the operation cannot exist. |
| Strip HTTP headers | redesigned | `http:strip-headers` | Bytes in, bytes out. Removes everything up to and including the first empty line (CRLF CRLF, LF LF or a mix of the two); a message that starts with an empty line has an empty header block. Differs from CyberChef, which returns the input unchanged when it finds no blank line: Forge raises E_COERCE (the header block is not closed), so a recipe notices a truncated message. The search is on the bytes as Latin-1, so any encoding and binary bodies work. |
| Dechunk HTTP response | redesigned | `http:dechunk` | Bytes in, bytes out. Decodes the chunked transfer coding of RFC 9112 section 7.1: hexadecimal chunk sizes, chunk extensions (skipped), the trailer fields (skipped) and the empty line that ends the message; a bare LF is accepted for CRLF. Stricter than CyberChef: empty input, a size that is not hex or runs past the data, a missing line end after the data, a missing last chunk or trailer end (truncation) and bytes after the end of the message are E_COERCE with the offset, where CyberChef stops at what it can read. Linear and bounded: the output is never longer than the input and a size is only compared with the bytes that are left. Run Strip HTTP headers first on a whole response. |
| Parse Ethernet frame | redesigned | `packets:parse-ethernet` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes, as in CyberChef. The result is text, one 'Name: value' line per field, not CyberChef's HTML table: the destination and source MAC (lower case, colons), every VLAN tag (IEEE 802.1Q TPID 0x8100 and 802.1ad 0x88a8, any number, each with priority, drop-eligible bit and VLAN ID), the EtherType with its registry name, or the length of an IEEE 802.3 frame when the field is 1500 or less, and the payload as hex. A frame shorter than 14 bytes (or a VLAN tag cut short) is E_COERCE with the offset. The field order follows CyberChef; the exact wording and the VLAN tag handling are from memory of CyberChef 11.5.0 and not verified against its code (the WP 5.59 cross-check does that). |
| Parse User Agent | redesigned | `user-agent:parse` | CyberChef's report layout (Browser, Device, Engine, OS and CPU, with unknown for what is not found) from a table of about 70 rules written in FL over the regex words, not the ua-parser-js library: version 2 of that library is AGPL, and version 1.x would put a library full of its own regular expressions outside the regex seam and add its size to the bundle. The table covers the common browsers, engines, systems, Apple, Samsung and Google devices (and the model in Android build strings), consoles, smart TVs and CPU architectures, so a rare or new agent can come out differently from ua-parser-js (the names follow that library: Mobile Safari, Samsung Internet, Chromium OS, Mac OS, amd64, ia32, arm64). The first rule that matches wins; a leading User-Agent: label is ignored; a string of more than 4,096 characters is E_RANGE. |
| Parse IP range | covered | `ip:parse-range` | A CIDR range, a hyphenated range or a list of addresses and CIDR ranges, IPv4 and IPv6, with CyberChef's three parameters (Include network info, Enumerate IP addresses, Allow large queries) and its report layout (Network, CIDR, Mask, Range, Total addresses; for a hyphenated range or a list the smallest holding subnet, tab-indented, then the range). The counts are exact (CyberChef adds IPv6 totals as floating point numbers) and IPv4 /32 is accepted (CyberChef stops at /31). Enumeration is IPv4 only, as in CyberChef. Where CyberChef puts a warning in the output for a range of more than 65,536 addresses, or prints that the second address is smaller, Forge raises E_RANGE; with Allow large queries the listing stops at 1,048,576 addresses (E_RANGE beyond), because the result must fit the value limit. Text that is not a range, a prefix length over 32 or 128, or a mix of IPv4 and IPv6 in a list is E_COERCE where CyberChef answers 'Invalid input'. |
| Parse IPv6 address | covered | `ip:parse-ipv6` | Longhand and shorthand (RFC 5952: the first longest run of two or more zero groups) and what the range is: unspecified, loopback, IPv4-mapped, IPv4-translated, discard, NAT64 (well-known and the RFC 8215 local-use prefix), Teredo (server, client address and port with the inversion undone and the obfuscated values, the cone, R, Random1, UG and Random2 flags, checked against RFC 4380 and RFC 5991), benchmarking, ORCHID v1 and v2, documentation, 6to4 (IPv4 address, SLA ID, interface ID in hex and decimal), unique local, link-local, multicast with the scope of the address and the well-known groups, plus ISATAP (RFC 5214) and the modified EUI-64 with its MAC address. The text is CyberChef's, with the additions (ISATAP, the scope of any multicast address, the Teredo obfuscated line, the RFC 8215 prefix, a Zone ID line); CyberChef's 6to4 interface ID and Teredo client address have arithmetic slips that Forge does not copy. The input may carry [brackets] and a %zone. An address that does not parse is E_COERCE where CyberChef answers 'Invalid IPv6 address'. |
| IPv6 Transition Addresses | covered | `ip:transition` | Per line: an IPv4 address to its 6to4 (2002:XXXX:XXXX::/48), IPv4-mapped, IPv4-translated and NAT64 forms; a 192.0.2.0/24 range with /40 and /120 (other prefix lengths are E_COERCE); a MAC address with colons to its modified EUI-64 interface identifier; and back from an IPv6 transition address (or an ISATAP address) to the IPv4 address, and from an EUI-64 address to the MAC. Both parameters, Ignore ranges (default on) and Remove headers (default off), are CyberChef's. CyberChef reads the IPv6 side with string slicing and glues the lines of a MAC address together; Forge parses the address and ends every line with a line feed. A line that is none of these is E_COERCE (CyberChef replaces the whole output with a message), and an IPv6 address with nothing embedded gets a line saying so. |
| Parse IPv4 header | redesigned | `packets:parse-ipv4` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes. Text with CyberChef's fields in its order (version, IHL with the byte length, DSCP, ECN, total length, identification in hex and decimal, the flags with each bit, fragment offset, TTL, protocol with its name, header checksum, source and destination address, options). Added: the header checksum is checked (valid, or invalid with the value it should have), the fragment offset also in bytes, and the options are decoded one per line (end of option list, no operation, others by name, kind, length and data in hex); an option with a missing, short or overlong length byte is E_COERCE. The header alone or a whole datagram is accepted and only the header is read. A header shorter than 20 bytes or than its IHL, a version other than 4 and an IHL below 5 are E_COERCE, where CyberChef prints what it can. The layout is from memory of CyberChef 11.5.0, not verified. |
| Strip IPv4 header | covered | `packets:strip-ipv4` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes; the output is the payload as bytes (use To Hex for hex text; CyberChef's own output type for this op was not verified). Drops IHL times 4 bytes, and also drops link padding after the datagram: the payload ends at the total length when that is set and the data holds that many bytes (a total length of 0, as with TCP segmentation offload, or one beyond the data keeps everything that is there). A header cut short, a version other than 4 and an IHL below 5 are E_COERCE. |
| Parse TCP | redesigned | `packets:parse-tcp` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes. Text: source and destination port, sequence and acknowledgement number, data offset (with the byte length), reserved bits, the nine flags (NS CWR ECE URG ACK PSH RST SYN FIN, summarised by name and one line each), window size, checksum as stored (not verified: that needs the IP addresses), urgent pointer, the options decoded (maximum segment size, window scale, SACK permitted, SACK blocks, timestamps, No-Operation, End of Option List; other kinds by name when known, with kind, length and data in hex) and the payload as hex. A header shorter than 20 bytes or than its data offset, a data offset below 5, an option with a missing, below-2 or overlong length byte, or a known kind with the wrong length, is E_COERCE with the offset. Field order and wording are from memory of CyberChef 11.5.0 (an HTML table) and not verified. |
| Strip TCP header | covered | `packets:strip-tcp` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes; the output is the payload as bytes: everything after the data offset times 4 bytes. A header cut short or a data offset below 5 is E_COERCE. |
| Parse TLS record | redesigned | `packets:parse-tls` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes; one or more records in a row. Text, a block per record separated by a blank line: content type, version, length; an alert with its level and description; handshake messages with their type and length and, for a ClientHello or ServerHello, the version, random, session ID, cipher suites with their IANA names (about 335 in the table), compression methods and extensions with their names, decoded for server_name, supported_groups, ec_point_formats, signature_algorithms, ALPN, supported_versions, psk_key_exchange_modes, key_share, compress_certificate, record_size_limit, padding and session_ticket (others as hex). GREASE values are named GREASE. SSL 3.0 and TLS 1.0 to 1.3 records are read; DTLS and SSL 2.0 are not TLS records. A message that goes on in the next record is shown with what is in the first record (messages are not joined across records). Anything that is not a TLS record, a record or hello cut short, lying lengths and damaged decoded extensions are E_COERCE with the offset. The hello reading is also shared words (packets:tls-records, tls-handshakes, tls-hellos) for the JA3 and JA4 ops of WP 5.54. The layout is Forge's own; CyberChef's was not verified. |
| Parse UDP | redesigned | `packets:parse-udp` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes. Text: source and destination port, length (a length beyond the data is shown with the number of bytes present; 0 means up to the end), checksum as stored (not verified) and the payload as hex, up to the length. A header shorter than 8 bytes or a length of 1 to 7 is E_COERCE. Field order from memory of CyberChef 11.5.0 (an HTML table), not verified. |
| Strip UDP header | covered | `packets:strip-udp` | Input format hex (default) or raw bytes; the output is the payload as bytes. The 8-byte header is dropped, and so is anything after the length the header declares (link padding); a length of 0 or beyond the data keeps all that is there. A header shorter than 8 bytes or a length of 1 to 7 is E_COERCE. |
| Parse URI | covered | `uri:parse` | CyberChef's layout (Protocol, Auth, Hostname, Port, Path name, Arguments, Hash; tab separated; the arguments padded and decoded as URLSearchParams does, a repeated one joined by commas) on the RFC 3986 reading: the authority is read after // and a port that is not digits is E_COERCE. The protocol is lower case with its colon, the host lower case, and for http, https, ftp, gopher, file, ws and wss with a host the path is at least /. CyberChef uses Node's legacy url.parse, which also reads a host from mailto:a@b.example and escapes spaces in the path; Forge does neither. The arguments appear in the order in which each name first appears (CyberChef puts integer-like names first). |
| Protobuf Decode | redesigned | `protobuf:decode` | Without a schema only: the .proto schema and Show Unknown Fields are not supported (not done in WP 5.54; they need a proto parser and a schema-driven reader). Show Types is show-types; added: indent (default 4, CyberChef's JSON output). JSON keyed by field number in ascending order, repeated fields as arrays, a length-delimited field read as a nested message when it parses completely (an empty one is {}), else UTF-8 text, else hex digits (CyberChef shows Latin-1 characters). Integers are exact (CyberChef's are doubles). Stricter: field number 0, a truncated field, a length past the data, a varint over 64 bits and the group wire types are E_COERCE with the offset (a nested guess fails on them instead); nesting is tried to 64 levels. The layout is from the CyberChef source (read for the layout only) and not cross-checked. |
| Protobuf Encode | not yet |  |  |
| VarInt Encode | redesigned | `varint:encode` | Decimal text in, bytes out (To Hex shows them). Unsigned 64-bit, exact; a negative number or one above 2^64 - 1 is E_RANGE and text that is not a whole decimal number is E_COERCE (CyberChef also reads 0x text and writes numbers of any size). Added: zigzag, for the signed protobuf types sint32 and sint64. |
| VarInt Decode | redesigned | `varint:decode` | Bytes in, decimal text out, exact. Exactly one VarInt of 1 to 10 bytes below 2^64: empty input, a truncated VarInt, one longer than 10 bytes or of 64 bits and more, and bytes after it are E_COERCE (CyberChef reads the first VarInt, ignores the rest and reads a truncated one as NaN). Added: zigzag. |
| JA3 Fingerprint | covered | `fingerprint:ja3` | Input format hex, base64 or raw; output hash digest (default), JA3 string or full details, with CyberChef's layouts (read from the 11.5.0 source). The JA3 string is Salesforce's: version, ciphers, extension types, groups and point formats, GREASE removed from the first four, MD5. Added: a bare ClientHello message is read as well as a record, and the first ClientHello of a flight of records is used. Stricter than CyberChef: a record that is not a TLS record, a hello that is cut short, a damaged extension or no ClientHello is E_COERCE with the offset (CyberChef needs exactly one record of the right length and does not look inside the extensions it does not read). Values checked against an independent Python implementation, not against CyberChef (the WP 5.59 cross-check does that). |
| JA3S Fingerprint | covered | `fingerprint:ja3s` | As JA3 Fingerprint for the ServerHello: version, chosen cipher and extension types (nothing removed), MD5; output hash digest, JA3S string or full details. A bare ServerHello message and the first ServerHello of a flight are read too; malformed input is E_COERCE. |
| JA4 Fingerprint | redesigned | `fingerprint:ja4` | Input format hex, base64 or raw; output JA4 (default), JA4 Original Rendering, JA4 Raw, JA4 Raw Original Rendering or All (the four labelled lines), as CyberChef. The fingerprint follows the FoxIO definition, and differs from CyberChef in two points that the FoxIO text decides: a list with no entries hashes to twelve zeros (CyberChef hashes the empty text) and the underscore and the signature algorithms are written only when the hello has the signature_algorithms extension (CyberChef always writes the underscore). Added: transport tcp (default, t) or quic (q) for the first character, and a bare ClientHello message is read too (a QUIC CRYPTO frame holds one; CyberChef does not read QUIC and always writes t). The original-order forms keep server_name and ALPN in the extension list as CyberChef's source builds them (not checked against the FoxIO page, which was not available offline). Verified with an independent Python implementation and the published Chrome fingerprint t13d1516h2_8daaf6152771_e5627efa2ab1, not against CyberChef. |
| JA4Server Fingerprint | covered | `fingerprint:ja4s` | Input format hex, base64 or raw; output JA4S (default), JA4S Raw or Both, as CyberChef: protocol, version (supported_versions or the version field), number of extensions, chosen ALPN, the chosen cipher, and the SHA-256 hash (12 hex digits, or twelve zeros for no extension) of the extension types in order. Added: the transport option and a bare ServerHello message; malformed input is E_COERCE. |
| HASSH Client Fingerprint | covered | `hassh:client` | Input format hex, base64 or raw: the SSH binary packet of SSH_MSG_KEXINIT sent by the client (exactly one packet, no MAC), as CyberChef takes it; output hash digest (default), HASSH algorithms string or full details, with CyberChef's layouts. kex;encryption c2s;mac c2s;compression c2s, MD5. Stricter than CyberChef: the name-lists must lie inside the payload and be printable US-ASCII, the padding at least 4 bytes and nothing may sit between the last field and the padding; each fault is E_COERCE with the offset. |
| HASSH Server Fingerprint | covered | `hassh:server` | As HASSH Client Fingerprint for the server's packet: kex;encryption s2c;mac s2c;compression s2c, MD5. |
| Format MAC addresses | covered | `mac:format` | CyberChef's parameters and layout: Output case (both, upper, lower), No delimiter, Dash delimiter, Colon delimiter, Cisco style and IPv6 interface ID, addresses cut at commas, white space and line feeds, a blank line after each address. The interface ID is the modified EUI-64 of RFC 4291 (ff fe inserted and the universal/local bit flipped), written as four groups. CyberChef has no validity check; Forge raises E_COERCE for anything that is not twelve hex digits (with or without : - . between them). |
| Group IP addresses | covered | `ip:group` | The layout is CyberChef's (network/prefix, the addresses indented by two spaces, a blank line), with its delimiters (newline, CRLF, space, comma, semicolon), prefix length (default 24) and Only show the subnets. Forge sorts the IPv4 addresses of a group by number (CyberChef sorts them as text), sorts the IPv6 networks and addresses (CyberChef does not), accepts a prefix length of 128, and refuses a piece that is not an address, and an IPv4 address with a prefix length over 32, with E_COERCE (CyberChef ignores the first and prints the second as /32 with the longer number). |

The second level (the DNS label form) is not part of the operation, as in CyberChef. |
| Decode NetBIOS Name | covered | `netbios:decode` | The inverse, with the same Offset (default 65): trailing spaces (the padding) are taken off, keeping the first byte. An odd length, more than 32 bytes or a byte outside offset to offset + 15 is E_COERCE where CyberChef returns nothing or a wrong byte. |
| Defang URL | covered | `defang:defang-url` | CyberChef's four parameters and patterns: Escape dots, Escape http, Escape ://, and Process (valid domains and full URLs, only full URLs, everything), with its URL and domain regular expressions. The process choices are named valid-domains-and-full-urls, only-full-urls and everything. |
| Fang URL | covered | `defang:fang-url` | Restore [.], restore hxxp (lower case only, as CyberChef) and restore [://], each switchable. |
| Defang IP Addresses | covered | `ip:defang` | IPv4 addresses (and a /prefix) get [.], IPv6 addresses get [:] (and [.] in an IPv4 tail). Forge finds an IPv6 address as a run of hex digits, colons and dots that parses as an address (CyberChef uses one long regular expression), and an IPv4 address only when it is not part of a longer dotted or numeric run (CyberChef would defang the first four numbers of 1.2.3.4.5). The word is in the ip vocabulary, because it uses the address parser. |

## Language (4)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unicode Text Format | covered | `unicode-format:decorate` | Underline (U+0332 COMBINING LOW LINE) and strikethrough (U+0336 COMBINING LONG STROKE OVERLAY), each switchable and off by default as in CyberChef (with both off the text is unchanged), put after every code point, the strikethrough mark first as CyberChef does. Line breaks get no marks. CyberChef adds the marks after every byte, so it breaks a character beyond ASCII; Forge adds them after every code point. |
| Remove Diacritics | covered | `diacritics:remove` | Unicode normalisation rather than a table of letters: NFD, drop the combining marks of the diacritic blocks (U+0300 to U+036F, U+1AB0 to U+1AFF, U+1DC0 to U+1DFF, U+20D0 to U+20FF, U+FE20 to U+FE2F), NFC again, so any script that decomposes is handled and other characters keep their form; the result equals CyberChef's. Letters with a stroke that do not decompose (o with stroke, d with stroke, eth, l with stroke, h with stroke, t with stroke, dotless i) are left alone by default, as CyberChef leaves them, and turned into their base letter with the strokes switch. Ligatures such as ae, oe and ss are left alone. |
| Convert to NATO alphabet | redesigned | `nato:encode`, `nato:decode` | The ICAO spelling alphabet (Alfa, Juliett, X-ray), letters in either case, digits plain (Zero, One, Two ...) as CyberChef writes them or as ICAO pronounces them (Wun, Too, Tree, Fower, Fife, Ait, Niner), and the way back as nato:decode, which also reads Alpha, Juliet, Xray and Whisky. Forge adds a delimiter (one of the wave 5 list except none) and writes a space as a slash so that words stay apart, with no trailing delimiter; other characters are kept, with the delimiter around them. CyberChef puts a space after every word, writes a space as an extra blank, and joins other characters to the next word without a space. |
| Convert Leet Speak | covered | `leet:convert` | To and from leet in one word. Basic is CyberChef's table: a4 e3 i1 o0 s5 t7, either case in, lower-case letters out of from. Extended is Forge's addition (b8 g6 z2 c( d) h# l\| q9 x%). Each letter has exactly one leet character, so from is a reading of the table, not an inverse; it cannot tell a leet 1 from a real 1. Non-ASCII text is left alone. |

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Diff | redesigned | `diff:compare` | Plain text instead of HTML: a unified-style diff by line (headers, hunks, context lines), and by word or character (the default, as in CyberChef) the second sample's text with [-deleted-] and {+inserted+} marks. Myers' shortest difference; ignore whitespace; the sentence, CSS and JSON modes, and the show added, removed and subtraction switches, are dropped. |

| Remove null bytes | covered | `clean:remove-null-bytes` |  |

It removes more than CyberChef's pattern, which leaves operating-system command strings (a window title), character set selections and the single-character escapes in place. |

| To Lower case | covered | `text:lower` |  |
| Swap case | covered | `case:swap-case` |  |
| Alternating Caps | covered | `case:alternating` | Starts with a lower case letter and counts letters only, as CyberChef does; adds a first parameter to start upper. |

| From Case Insensitive Regex | redesigned | `case:from-insensitive-regex` | The inverse of case:to-insensitive-regex: a class with both cases of a letter becomes the first one, so [hH] is h as in CyberChef. A class that holds one plain letter ([b]) loses its brackets, and the second case in bigger classes is dropped ([a-zA-Z0-9] is [a-z0-9]). |
| Add line numbers | covered | `lines:add-numbers` | The number right-aligned to the width of the count of lines (so the width does not grow with the offset, as CyberChef's), a space, the line. The delimiter is a choice. |
| Remove line numbers | covered | `lines:remove-numbers` | Works line by line with the same pattern (up to 5 spaces or tabs, digits, one separator character: white space or one of : \| - , . ) ]). CyberChef lets the separator match a line feed, so a line holding only a number swallows the line break and joins the next line; Forge never joins lines, and a line of digits only is left as it is. |
| Get All Casings | redesigned | `case:all-casings` | Only letters with a case are varied (at most 12, so at most 4,096 lines) instead of every character: CyberChef writes the same line several times for a character without a case. | To Table | covered | `lines:to-table` | ASCII box and Markdown pipe table, in CyberChef's layouts (a rule above the rows, under the header row when the header switch is on and below the last row, no rule between rows; for Markdown the first row is always the header, dashes as wide as the column; every line ends with a line feed). The HTML format is dropped (Forge shows text only). The cell and row delimiters are choices from the shared list rather than free text, and a double-quoted cell may hold the cell delimiter (not a row delimiter). Short rows are filled with empty cells (CyberChef draws them short, or drops a one-cell last row), text is not HTML-escaped, and a \| in a Markdown cell is escaped. An empty input is an empty output. |
| Reverse | covered | `text:reverse` |  |
| Sort | redesigned | `lines:sort` | One word with the delimiter, reverse and the six orders. Strings are compared by code point where CyberChef uses the host's locale compare (so the case-insensitive and IP-address orders put e and z in a different order from CyberChef on non-ASCII text, and A, a and b are ordered by code point in the ties); numeric reads a decimal at the start of the line without an exponent (CyberChef compares chunks of digits and text, which orders a leading minus sign and mixed lines differently), hexadecimal a hex number at the start, IP address puts text that is not four decimal fields of 0 to 255 after the addresses in code point order; pieces with equal numbers, or no number, are in code point order. The alphabetical and length orders are stable. |
| Shuffle | covered | `lines:shuffle` | A uniform Fisher-Yates shuffle on the host's cryptographic random generator (+random); the delimiter is a choice from the shared list. |
| Unique | covered | `lines:unique` | Keeps the first of each in place. With show-count each line is written as its count, a space and the line, in the order of first appearance (CyberChef lists them in the order of a JavaScript object, which puts the lines that look like whole numbers first). |
| Split | covered | `text:split` |  |

| Tail | covered | `lines:tail` | A negative number keeps all but the first \|number\| lines. A number of 0 keeps none (CyberChef returns everything for 0). |

A padding of several characters is repeated and cut like padStart. |
| Find / Replace | covered | `text:replace`, `regex:replace` | Literal replacement in text:replace, pattern replacement in regex:replace. |
| Regular expression | covered | `regex:find-all`, `regex:test` | Matches come back as records (start, end, text); regex:test is the yes/no form. |
| Fuzzy Match | redesigned | `search:fuzzy` | A text report instead of highlighted HTML: one row per matching line with a score, the matched positions and the line, scored by a documented greedy rule rather than CyberChef's Sublime-style matcher. |
| Offset checker | redesigned | `search:offsets` | A text report instead of highlighting: one row per stretch of offsets where all samples share the same character (offset, length, text). |

Raw text is compared as UTF-8 bytes (CyberChef compares UTF-16 characters), samples of different length are E_COERCE, as in CyberChef, and so are hex samples with an odd number of digits or a non-hex digit (CyberChef reads them leniently). |
| Levenshtein Distance | covered | `distance:levenshtein` | Over code points (CyberChef counts UTF-16 characters, so a character beyond the BMP costs 2 there); the dynamic programme is a private primitive (limit 100 million cells). Costs for insertion, deletion and substitution, as CyberChef. |
| Convert distance | redesigned | `units:convert-distance` | Forge-native unit names (metre, kilometre, inch, nautical-mile, astronomical-unit, light-year, and so on) instead of CyberChef's menu, with a source and a target unit. The sum is exact: every unit is an exact ratio of the metre (international yard of 1959, NIST SP 811), the value is decimal text with an optional sign and exponent, and the result is rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (20 by default, as CyberChef) and written in plain decimal form. The ratios agree with CyberChef's except the fathom and the nautical mile: CyberChef's fathom is 1.853184 m and its nautical mile 1,853.184 m, where the fathom is 6 feet (1.8288 m) and the nautical mile 1,852 m by definition. No parsec (it is not a rational number of metres), and none of the comparison units (cars, football fields). A value that is not a number is E_COERCE. |
| Convert area | redesigned | `units:convert-area` | Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Exact ratios of the square metre (the acre is 4046.8564224 m2); CyberChef's nuclear-physics and comparison units are not offered. |
| Convert mass | redesigned | `units:convert-mass` | Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Exact ratios of the kilogram (the international pound is 0.45359237 kg; the grain, carat and troy ounce are exact); the archaic and comparison units are not offered. |
| Convert speed | redesigned | `units:convert-speed` | Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Exact ratios of the metre per second (the knot is 1852 m per hour, the mile per hour 0.44704 m/s, kilometre per hour 1/3.6): CyberChef's factors are rounded (0.2778 m/s for a kilometre per hour, 1.6092 km/h for a mile per hour, a knot of 1.8517 km/h), so its results differ from the fourth digit. Mach is not offered, because it depends on the air, and neither are the comparison and scientific speeds. |
| Convert data units | redesigned | `units:convert-data` | Same design as Convert distance: Forge-native unit names, exact ratios of the base unit, and the result rounded half away from zero to a number of decimal places (the digits parameter, 20 by default, as CyberChef's BigNumber rounds). Bits, nibbles, bytes, the decimal units (kilo to exa, powers of 1000) and the binary units (kibi to exbi, IEC 80000-13, powers of 1024), as bits and as bytes. Equal to CyberChef's for the units both have, except that CyberChef rounds its conversion factors, so from the 17th digit on (petabyte or exabyte to exbibyte) its results are off; Forge has no deca-, hecto-, zetta- or yotta- units. |
| Convert co-ordinate format | redesigned | `coords:convert` | One op with a source format (auto detects it), a target format and a precision. Formats: decimal degrees, degrees and decimal minutes, degrees minutes and seconds, geohash, UTM and MGRS (WGS 84, 80 S to 84 N; Karney's series, sub-millimetre). Degrees convert exactly (whole numbers of 10^-12 degree). The Ordnance Survey National Grid is not offered: it needs the OSGB36 datum shift, which cannot be done exactly from a published formula. CyberChef's delimiter and direction menus are replaced by a reader that accepts any separator and the letters N S E W before or after the numbers; the output always writes the hemisphere letters (degrees notations) or a sign (decimal degrees). MGRS and geohash input is read as the middle of its cell. |
| Show on map | dropped |  | It draws a map from tiles fetched from an external tile host. Forge's CSP allows only its own origin (connect-src 'self', no external img-src) and the app never talks to another host, so the operation cannot exist. The coordinates themselves are covered by the co-ordinate format and Haversine distance operations. |
| Parse UNIX file permissions | covered | `file-mode:parse`, `file-mode:convert` | file-mode:parse writes CyberChef's report: Textual representation, Octal representation, the File type line when a type character was given, the set-user-ID, set-group-ID and sticky bit lines, and the box with an X for each read, write and execute bit. It reads an octal mode of three or four digits (CyberChef also reads one or two, which it takes as the user and group digits), or symbolic text with or without the type character (CyberChef needs the type character). file-mode:convert only changes the notation (octal or symbolic). |
| Parse ObjectID timestamp | covered | `objectid:timestamp` | The first 8 hex digits of the 24-digit ObjectID as seconds since the epoch, written as an ISO 8601 UTC time with a .000 fraction. |
| Parse colour code | redesigned | `colour:parse` | Reads hex (3, 4, 6 or 8 digits, with or without #), rgb()/rgba(), hsl()/hsla() and cmyk() and writes a text report of hex, RGB, RGBA, HSL, HSLA and CMYK with whole-number channels; CyberChef also draws a colour swatch, and Forge's ops return text. Colour names are not read. |
| Escape string | covered | `string-escape:escape` | Forge's escaper, written in FL, follows the rules of the library CyberChef uses, found by comparing outputs over every level, quote, JSON, ES6 and upper-case combination: levels special, everything and minimal; quote single, double or backtick; the short escapes \b \t \n \f \r, \0 (not before a digit), \xHH, \uHHHH, \u{H}, the vertical tab as \x0b, and with JSON on the chosen quote put around the text. Forge text is made of Unicode scalar values, so a lone surrogate cannot occur. |
