## Date / Time (9)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Parse DateTime | redesigned | `datetime:parse` | The same report (date, time, AM or PM, time zone, UTC offset, daylight saving, leap year, days in the month, day of the year, week number, quarter). Forge has no populate-the-box control, so the built-in formats are a preset choice and the format string applies with the preset Custom. Reading is forgiving like moment.js but a literal of the format is used up only when it is the next text, and fields the format does not name default to 1970-01-01 00:00 (not today). The week number is the ISO week. The zone abbreviation comes from the host's Intl data (it can read GMT+9 where a time zone database says JST). Written in FL with Forge's own moment.js-style tokens and no date library; only the zone rules come from the host. |
| Translate DateTime Format | redesigned | `datetime:translate` | Input format, input zone, output format and output zone as in CyberChef, with the built-in formats as a preset choice per side (Custom uses the format string). The tokens are Forge's own moment.js-compatible set (YYYY to SSSSSSSSS, Z, z, X, x, W, G, L, [literal] and so on); the SSS tokens keep the full nanosecond and z comes from the host's Intl data. No date library. |
| From UNIX Timestamp | covered | `datetime:from-unix` | Units are seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds; the default output is CyberChef's (Wed 11 November 2026 12:34:56 UTC for seconds, and with .SSS for the other units, whose milliseconds are shown). Instead of the Treat as UTC switch there is a zone parameter and a format string, so the time can be written in any zone and any format. Whole and decimal numbers, negative allowed, exact to the nanosecond. Text that is not a number is E_COERCE (CyberChef writes Invalid date). |
| To UNIX Timestamp | redesigned | `datetime:to-unix` | Units and Show parsed datetime (on by default, as in CyberChef) as there. CyberChef lets moment.js guess the input format; Forge reads a stated format (default YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss, forgiving, so an ISO 8601 text like 2026-11-11T12:34:56Z reads) in a zone parameter that replaces Treat as UTC. Rounded down to a whole number in the unit. |
| Windows Filetime to UNIX Timestamp | covered | `datetime:filetime-to-unix` | Input decimal, hex big endian or hex little endian; output seconds, milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds, exact as CyberChef's (up to seven decimals for seconds, four for milliseconds, one for microseconds, no trailing zeros). Argument order is input then unit, and the choices are lower case (decimal, hex-be, hex-le); an optional 0x and spaces are accepted. |
| UNIX Timestamp to Windows Filetime | covered | `datetime:unix-to-filetime` | Input unit and output decimal, hex big endian or hex little endian (lower-case choices decimal, hex-be, hex-le). The big-endian hex has no leading zeros, as CyberChef writes it; the little-endian form is always 16 digits (the 8 bytes). A time before 1601 or past the 64-bit range is E_RANGE. Decimal timestamps are accepted and a fraction finer than 100 ns is cut (CyberChef keeps it as a fraction of a tick). |
| DateTime Delta | covered | `datetime:delta` | Add or subtract days, hours, minutes and seconds (and milliseconds, which CyberChef lacks) from a date in a preset or custom format, written back in that format. A zone parameter is added (UTC by default, as in CyberChef); days are calendar days there, the rest elapsed time. Negative amounts reverse the direction. |
| Extract dates | redesigned | `datetime:extract-dates` | yyyy-mm-dd, dd/mm/yyyy and mm/dd/yyyy dates with - / . or space between the parts, one per line, with Display total, Sort and Unique as in CyberChef. Forge writes its own pattern: months and days of one or two digits, years 1900 to 2099, word boundaries on both sides, and a month-first date is found when the day is above 12. Nothing is checked beyond the pattern (2026-02-30 is listed). |
| Get Time | covered | `clock:get-time` | The time since the Unix epoch in seconds (the default, as in CyberChef), milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds, as decimal text. The host clock counts milliseconds, so the finer units are that count times 1,000 and 1,000,000 and the extra digits are zero. Seconds are rounded down (CyberChef rounds to the nearest second). The input is ignored. |

## Extractors (18)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strings | redesigned | `extract:strings` | Encoding single, utf16le, utf16be or all; minimum length; the character class is alphanumeric plus punctuation (the default, CyberChef's first choice, with the same punctuation) or printable (space to tilde), with a null-terminated switch instead of CyberChef's third class; the Unicode (non-ASCII) classes are not offered; display total, sort and unique as in CyberChef (unique keeps the first appearance, then sort, then the total). The UTF-16 zero bytes and a null terminator are not part of the output (CyberChef leaves them in). Input is read as bytes. |
| Extract IP addresses | covered | `extract:ip-addresses` | IPv4, IPv6 and remove-local as in CyberChef (the local ranges are 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 and 127/8); display total, sort and unique. Forge's own patterns: leading zeros are accepted, an address that is part of a longer dotted number is not found, IPv6 is found in all the forms of RFC 4291 (CyberChef finds only the full eight-group form and its simple shortenings), and the sort is by code point. |
| Extract email addresses | redesigned | `extract:emails` | Forge's own pattern, ASCII only: quoted local parts and non-ASCII (internationalised) addresses are not found, and a host needs two or more labels. |
| Extract MAC addresses | redesigned | `extract:mac-addresses` | Colon and hyphen forms as in CyberChef, plus the dotted Cisco form; a match inside a longer run of hex pairs is not found. |
| Extract URLs | redesigned | `extract:urls` | Any scheme with ://, user information, IPv6 hosts in brackets; trailing punctuation and unpaired closing brackets are left out, round brackets in pairs stay. Forge's own pattern, so edge cases differ from CyberChef's. |
| Extract domains | redesigned | `extract:domains` | Forge's own pattern with CyberChef's Underscore option (off by default: a label with an underscore is then not part of a name). The option to show only valid top-level domains is not offered (it needs the list of top-level domains): the last label only has to be letters (or xn--), so file names such as report.txt are found too. A name after a dot or inside a longer word is not read from its middle (CyberChef finds example.com in _dmarc.example.com). |
| Extract file paths | redesigned | `extract:file-paths` | Windows and UNIX switches as in CyberChef. Forge's own patterns: a Windows folder name may hold single spaces but the last name stops at the first space; a UNIX path ends at white space and is not found inside a word, a URL or a relative path. |
| Extract hashes | redesigned | `extract:hashes` | A length from 1 to 128 hex digits (40 by default), or all, which finds the digest sizes 4, 8, 16, 32, 40, 48, 56, 64, 80, 96 and 128 digits with the values of each size together, the shortest size first, as CyberChef does (CyberChef also takes runs of 1 and 2 digits as hashes, which Forge does not); a run must not touch other letters, digits or underscores. |
| XPath expression | covered | `xpath:query` | The xpath and @xmldom/xmldom libraries as CyberChef uses them: an XPath 1.0 expression over XML text, every selected node written as markup and joined with the result delimiter (escapes read, default \n), a name with no prefix matching any namespace. Added: an expression that gives a number, string or boolean writes that value (CyberChef fails). Attributes are written name="value". Bounds: expression length 4096 (E_RANGE), documents nested deeper than 512 levels or with more than 200,000 nodes and output past the value limit are E_LIMIT_VALUE; declared entities are not expanded and external entities are never read; some expressions are slow on a large document (a chain of ancestor:: and descendant:: steps took ten seconds on 64 KiB) and are stopped by the host's hard time limit. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): xpath 0.0.34 with @xmldom/xmldom 0.8.15 run on five expressions: identical except that xmldom writes an attribute with a leading space (' x="1"') and Forge without, and a number result is an error there. |
| JPath expression | redesigned | `jsonpath:query` | The query language is RFC 9535 JSONPath (the json-p3 library, which passes the whole JSONPath Compliance Test Suite) instead of the Goessner dialect of jsonpath-plus, which evaluates script expressions with an interpreter of its own or with new Function and does not accept the RFC's filter syntax. The common queries are the same ($.store.book[*].author, $..price, $..book[?(@.price<10)], [0,1], [-1:], [:2]); script expressions [(@.length-1)] and the ^ ~ @path @property extensions are E_COERCE. Parameters and output as CyberChef: the query, a result delimiter (escapes read, default \n), every match as compact JSON text. A query that selects nothing gives an empty result. Own members only are read (a key named constructor or __proto__ is an ordinary key); integers beyond 2^53 are selected exactly but a filter comparing one never matches. Bounds: query length 4096 (E_RANGE), filters nested 30 deep and descent deeper than 512 levels (E_LIMIT_VALUE), results held to the value limit; an expensive query on a large document is stopped by the host's hard time limit. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): jsonpath-plus 10.4.0 run on five queries ($.store.book[*].author, $..price, a filter, $.a, $..*): identical result text. |
| Jsonata Query | covered | `jsonata:query` | The jsonata library (IBM, MIT) as CyberChef uses it, parameter and output as CyberChef (the result as compact JSON text, nothing selected is the empty string). The primitive is asynchronous (version 2 of the library is). Deliberate differences: $random, $shuffle, $now and $millis raise an error (ops take randomness and time only from the random and clock vocabularies), $pad is limited to 1,000,000 characters, and evaluation is counted and bounded: more than 3,000,000 evaluation steps is E_LIMIT_STEPS, nesting past 1,000 levels, a sequence past 1,000,000 items and a range past 10 million are E_LIMIT_VALUE; integers beyond 2^53 lose precision as in JavaScript; a result that is a function is E_COERCE. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): jsonata 2.2 run on four queries: identical text; the default query (string) is CyberChef's. |
| CSS selector | redesigned | `css:select` | The HTML is read by htmlparser2 (which repairs bad markup like a browser and never fails), matched by css-select (CSS Selectors level 4) and written by dom-serializer, instead of xmldom and nwmatcher, which fail on HTML that is not XML. Parameters as CyberChef: the selector and a delimiter (escapes read, default \n); the outer HTML of each match in document order, nested matches listed again inside their parent; an empty selector or document gives an empty result. Matches are written as HTML (<br>, attribute values in double quotes, & < > as entities, other characters as they are). A pseudo-element, an unknown pseudo-class or a syntax error is E_COERCE. Bounds: selector length 4096 (E_RANGE), documents nested deeper than 512 levels or with more than 200,000 nodes and output past the value limit are E_LIMIT_VALUE. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read (nwmatcher needs a DOM and was not run); the empty-selector and empty-input rule and the delimiter are CyberChef's. |
| Extract EXIF | redesigned | `exif:extract` | Found N tags. and a blank line, then Name: value for the tags of IFD0, the Exif IFD with the Interoperability IFD, the GPS IFD and the thumbnail IFD (names start with Thumbnail:), read without decoding the image, from a JPEG (the APP1 Exif segment), a PNG (eXIf), a WebP (EXIF) or a bare TIFF, in either byte order. The tag names are Pillow's ExifTags (TIFF 6, Exif 2.32, GPS). Values are the numbers stored, not translated words (Orientation: 1); rationals are decimals with up to six places, arrays show their first 16 values, the maker note is named by its size and not decoded, user comments are decoded by their character prefix, Windows XP tags are UTF-16, FLOAT and DOUBLE values are shown as hex. A JPEG without Exif gives Found 0 tags.; other data, a damaged TIFF structure or a value that runs past the data is E_COERCE. CyberChef's library (exif-parser) names tags and formats values differently in places (and gives GPS as decimal degrees). Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the layout (Found N tags. and a blank line, then Name: value per tag) is CyberChef's; the tag names and value formats are not. Verified against Pillow's Image.Exif reader on files from an independent TIFF writer. |
| Extract ID3 | redesigned | `id3:extract` | ID3v2.2, 2.3 and 2.4 at the start of the data and ID3v1 and v1.1 in the last 128 bytes, as text in Forge's own layout (one line per frame: Identifier (name): value; the flags unsynchronisation, extended header and footer in the heading). Text frames by their encoding byte (ISO-8859-1, UTF-16 with or without a mark, UTF-8, surrogate pairs), TXXX, WXXX, comments, lyrics, APIC and PIC (MIME type, picture type, size, description), PRIV, UFID, POPM, PCNT, GEOB; genres by number get the ID3v1 name (0 to 147). The whole-tag unsynchronisation of v2.3, the extended header and padding are handled; a frame with compression or encryption is named and not decoded; other frames show their size. No tag gives 'No ID3 tag found.'; a tag or frame that runs past the data is E_COERCE with the offset; at most 1,000 frames. ffprobe reads the same text fields (it cannot read the v2.3 whole-tag unsynchronisation). Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): CyberChef's op reads only an ID3v2 tag at the start, with its own crude parser (the frame data as Latin-1 after skipping one byte, v2.2 frames mishandled, an unknown frame is an error), returns JSON ({Type, Version, Flags, Size, Tags: {id: {Size, Description, Data}}}) and shows it as an HTML table of Tag, Description and Data. Forge keeps its text, one line per frame, which carries the same fields (the identifier, a description and the decoded value) for more versions and encodings; the outputs are not the same shape, as a deliberate difference. |
| Extract Audio Metadata | redesigned | `audio-meta:extract` | Container metadata without decoding audio, as lines of Name: value and a Tags: block: MP3 (MPEG version and layer, bit rate, sample rate, channels, duration from the Xing, Info or VBRI frame count or else from the bit rate, and the ID3 tags as Extract ID3 shows them), FLAC (STREAMINFO, Vorbis comments, pictures), Ogg (Vorbis, Opus, Speex: identification packet, comment packet over several pages, duration from the last granule position), WAV (fmt, data size, LIST INFO) and MP4 or M4A (ftyp, mvhd, the audio sample entry, ilst tags and cover art size). Sample rate, channels and duration were compared with ffprobe on files from ffmpeg (Opus: the pre-skip is subtracted, as the specification says). Not read: APE, WavPack, AIFF, ASF, tags inside Ogg FLAC streams, chapter and cue data, Matroska. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): CyberChef's op has its own parsers for MP3, WAV and BW64, FLAC, Ogg, MP4, AIFF, AAC, AC3 and WMA, takes a file name and a maximum size of embedded text as parameters and returns a normalised JSON report (container, tags, technical, embedded objects, errors) shown as an HTML table. Forge keeps its text report and has no parameters; AIFF, AAC, AC3 and ASF/WMA are not read here (see above), and the JSON shape is not reproduced. |
| Extract Files | redesigned | `filetype:extract`, `filetype:entry` | The files found by signature, cut out with an end finder per type where the format allows one: PNG (to IEND), JPEG (segments to EOI), GIF (blocks to the trailer), BMP and RIFF (WAV, AVI, WebP) by the size field, ICO, PDF (the last %%EOF before the next %PDF-), RTF (balanced braces), ZIP and its relatives (the end record whose directory closes exactly at that record, so a stored zip inside a zip is told from its container), 7z, gzip (the existing inflate, then the trailer), Zstandard (block walk), tar (header checksums), cab, DEX, SQLite, pcap and pcapng, DER certificates, PEM, MP4 boxes, Ogg pages, EBML segments, ELF and PE (sizes from the headers; a PE overlay is not included). A type with no end finder (TIFF, FLAC, MP3, RAR, bzip2, xz, Mach-O, OLE2, ...) or a damaged or cut-short file has no end finder and is always left out, as CyberChef does (No extraction algorithm available is never an error); a damaged or cut-short file is left out with Ignore failed extractions (the default, as CyberChef) and is E_COERCE otherwise; nothing falls back to 'to the next signature'. Added: Minimum File Size (default 100, as CyberChef's) leaves out smaller files. The result is a list of records (name extracted_at_0x<offset>.<ext>, offset, size, type = the MIME type, data) in the Wave 7 archive convention, and filetype:entry returns one by index as bytes so that a recipe can go on. Miscellaneous is off by default as in CyberChef. Nested files are extracted as well; the total is bounded by the value limit (E_LIMIT_VALUE) and the work of the end finders by 2^28 bytes examined. Category Forensics (CyberChef files it under both Extractors and Forensics). Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read; the file names (extracted_at_0x<offset>.<ext>), the order, the options and their defaults are CyberChef's; the result is a list of records instead of a list of File objects with an HTML preview. |
| RAKE | redesigned | `rake:keywords` | RAKE of Rose et al. 2010 with Forge's own English stop list (replaceable by a comma or white space separated list), a maximum phrase length (3 by default; CyberChef has none) instead of regular-expression delimiters, and a limit. The output is one line per phrase: its score (two decimals), a colon, a space and the phrase, highest score first, equal scores in alphabetical order. CyberChef writes Scores: , Keywords: , then score, phrase lines with the scores as plain numbers, and keeps punctuation attached to the words (so strict inequations, and strict inequations are different phrases there); Forge's words are letters, digits and marks with an inner apostrophe or hyphen, and every other character ends a phrase, so the keywords and scores differ. |
| Template | redesigned | `template:render` | A documented subset of Handlebars rendered by a tree walker written for Forge, because Handlebars compiles templates to JavaScript and runs them with new Function (code execution, impossible under the strict CSP). Supported: {{x}} (HTML-escaped as Handlebars does), {{{x}}}, {{& x}}, comments, \{{ escapes, paths (a.b, a/b, this, ../, a.[b c], length, @root @index @key @first @last), if (with else if, includeZero), unless, each (lists and objects, else, block parameters), with, lookup, Mustache sections and inverted sections, white-space control {{~x~}} and the standalone-line rule; the output equals Handlebars 4.7.10 on 3,700 random templates and the 56 vectors. Not supported (E_COERCE with the line and column): partials, decorators, raw blocks, custom helpers, log. Only own properties are read. Bounds: blocks nested 100 deep (E_LIMIT_VALUE), 5,000,000 render steps (E_LIMIT_STEPS), output held to the value limit. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): CyberChef's Template is Handlebars.compile(template)(json) and so HTML-escapes {{x}} as well (it does not render plain text only, as its description says); Handlebars 4.7.x run on four templates, identical output. |

## Compression (21)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Raw Deflate | redesigned | `deflate:deflate` | RFC 1951 over fflate (a private primitive for the entropy coding). CyberChef's Compression type menu (Dynamic Huffman Coding, Fixed Huffman Coding, None) becomes the wave 6 level parameter, an int from 0 to 9 (else E_RANGE), default 6: None is level 0 (stored blocks, byte for byte what zlib writes up to 65,531 bytes; Forge writes blocks of 65,535 bytes, zlib cuts longer inputs differently), Dynamic Huffman Coding is any level from 1 (fflate chooses a stored, fixed or dynamic block for each block by size, so very short input comes out as a fixed block); a Fixed-only mode does not exist. Every inflater reads the output (checked against zlib), but the bytes differ from CyberChef's zlib.js encoder. Cross-checked (wave 6 close-out, CyberChef 11.5.0): everything CyberChef writes in all three compression types reads here, and everything written here at levels 0 to 9 reads in CyberChef, except that CyberChef writes an invalid stream for an empty input in the Fixed and None types (no end-of-block code). |
| Raw Inflate | redesigned | `deflate:inflate` | RFC 1951 over fflate. Start index is kept (start, from 0; beyond the input is E_RANGE); bytes after the end of the stream are ignored. Initial output buffer size, Buffer expansion type and Resize buffer after decompression tuned zlib.js's buffers and mean nothing here (the primitive manages its own), and Verify result has nothing to verify in a raw stream, so those four are not offered. Corrupt or cut-short data is E_COERCE naming the fault; output past the value limit (16 MiB for shared recipes, 64 MiB otherwise) stops with E_LIMIT_VALUE instead of allocating, the decompression bomb rule of the wave 6 conventions. Cross-checked with CyberChef 11.5.0 at the wave 6 close-out: reads everything its Raw Deflate writes in the three compression types (the empty input in the Fixed and None types excepted: CyberChef writes an unterminated stream there), and CyberChef reads what this writes at levels 0 to 9. |
| Zlib Deflate | redesigned | `deflate:zlib-deflate` | RFC 1950: the two header bytes (78 01, 78 5e, 78 9c or 78 da as zlib writes them for the level), the raw stream and the big-endian Adler-32, the framing in FL over adler32:checksum. Compression type is the level parameter as in Raw Deflate (0 to 9, default 6; no Fixed-only mode). The output bytes differ from CyberChef's, and every zlib reads them. Cross-checked: the two header bytes equal CyberChef's (78 9c for Dynamic, 78 5e for Fixed = levels 2 to 5 here, 78 01 for None = level 0), and a stored stream of up to 65,531 bytes equals CyberChef's byte for byte. |
| Zlib Inflate | redesigned | `deflate:zlib-inflate` | RFC 1950 in FL over the raw inflate: the header is checked (not zlib, another method, a window over 32 KiB, a preset dictionary: E_COERCE) and the Adler-32 trailer is verified. Start index is kept; Verify result is verify and is on by default (CyberChef's is off): a missing or wrong trailer is E_COERCE, and with verify off the trailer is not read. The buffer size, expansion and resize options are not offered (see Raw Inflate). Output past the value limit is E_LIMIT_VALUE. The checksums are primitives (crc:_crc, adler32:_adler), so a 16 MiB gzip or zlib stream is a few hundred VM steps, inside the default and the untrusted limits. Cross-checked: reads every CyberChef Zlib Deflate stream with the Adler-32 verified. |
| Gzip | redesigned | `deflate:gzip` | RFC 1952 in FL over the raw deflate and crc:checksum: the header, the optional file name and comment (Latin-1; a NUL or a character above U+00FF is E_RANGE), the optional header CRC-16 (CyberChef's Include file checksum, parameter header-crc), the raw stream and the little-endian CRC-32 and size. Compression type is the level (0 to 9, default 6). Added: mtime, the modification time in Unix seconds, 0 by default so the output is the same on every run (CyberChef writes the current time); the OS byte is 255 (unknown) and XFL follows the level as gzip writes it. The bytes differ from CyberChef's; gzip, Python and zlib read them. Cross-checked: with the same mtime the header (flags for name, comment and header CRC-16, the OS byte 255, even the CRC-16 value) equals CyberChef's byte for byte; the differences are the XFL byte, which follows the level here (CyberChef always writes 0), and the mtime. CyberChef reads every output here (levels 0 to 9, name, comment, header CRC). |
| Gunzip | covered | `deflate:gunzip` | RFC 1952: the header (extra field, name, comment and header CRC-16 are read and skipped; a missing magic number, another method or reserved flags are E_COERCE), the stream, and the CRC-32 and size of the trailer, which are verified by default (the added parameter verify, on; off returns the data despite a bad trailer or header CRC). Members written one after the other are joined, as gzip does. Output past the value limit is E_LIMIT_VALUE; the size the trailer claims is never used to allocate. Cross-checked: reads CyberChef's Gzip output with name, comment and header CRC-16 in all three compression types, checksums verified. |
| Zip | redesigned | `zip:zip` | PKWARE APPNOTE container in FL (local header, central directory, end record) over crc:checksum and deflate:deflate (the CRC-32 and the DEFLATE encoder are primitives); one file, as in CyberChef (the filename parameter, default file.txt; the file type does not exist yet). Comment (a file comment in the central directory), Compression method (method: deflate or store) and Operating system (os: msdos, unix or macintosh; the default is msdos, the first of CyberChef's list) are kept. Compression type becomes the level parameter (0 to 9, default 6; 0 stores in DEFLATE blocks; Fixed Huffman Coding is not offered, as for Raw Deflate). Added: mtime (Unix seconds, DOS precision, 0 by default meaning 1980-01-01 so the output is the same on every run; CyberChef writes the current time) and mode (the Unix permission bits, stored when os is unix). Password (ZipCrypto) is not supported. The compressed bytes differ from CyberChef's (a different encoder); unzip, Python and fflate read them. Cross-checked (CyberChef 11.5.0, the clock fixed): the archive for Macintosh as the operating system is byte for byte CyberChef's for a short file; CyberChef's Unzip, with Verify on, reads archives written here for both methods, all three operating systems, levels 0, 1, 6 and 9 and names with a directory. Differences: the version needed is 10 for a stored entry here (CyberChef writes 20), the Unix attributes are written here (CyberChef leaves them 0), and a name is UTF-8 here where CyberChef reads and writes it as Latin-1 (a non-ASCII name looks garbled in CyberChef). CyberChef's Fixed and None compression types write an invalid entry for an empty file. |
| Unzip | redesigned | `zip:unzip`, `zip:entry` | Returns a list of records (name, size, dir, mtime, mode, data) in directory order, which the output pane shows as a tree, instead of CyberChef's list of files; mtime reads the DOS time as UTC and mode is the Unix permission bits for entries made on Unix (else 0). zip:entry (not a CyberChef row) takes one entry's bytes by name so a recipe can continue, and inflates only that entry. The central directory is read, so streamed archives (data descriptors) and archives with bytes in front work. Stored and deflate only; any other method, an encrypted entry, ZIP64 or a multi-disk archive is E_COERCE naming it, so CyberChef's Password is not supported. Verify result is verify and is on by default (CyberChef's is off): each entry's size and CRC-32 must match (E_COERCE), off returns damaged data. The sum of all entries is capped by the value limit while they are inflated (E_LIMIT_VALUE), whatever sizes the archive claims. No extra keys such as a comment. Cross-checked: reads every archive CyberChef's Zip writes (both methods, three operating systems, three compression types, names with directories, with a comment), with the sizes and CRC-32 verified. |
| Bzip2 Decompress | redesigned | `bzip2:decompress` | The bzip2 format written from its specification (inverse BWT, MTF, Huffman, run-length step, randomised blocks, block and stream CRC-32). Several streams one after the other are joined, as bzip2 -d does; bytes after the last stream that do not start another are ignored. Added: verify, on by default, checks every CRC (E_COERCE otherwise); off, a bad checksum is ignored. CyberChef's low-memory option (use a slower algorithm in libbzip2) has no meaning here and is not offered. Corrupt or cut-short data is E_COERCE naming the fault; a block larger than its header's block size allows is E_COERCE; output past the value limit (16 MiB for shared recipes, 64 MiB otherwise) stops with E_LIMIT_VALUE while decoding. CyberChef also rejects an empty input; here an empty input is E_COERCE as not bzip2 data. Cross-checked: decompresses everything CyberChef's Bzip2 Compress writes at block sizes 1, 2, 5 and 9 and work factors 0, 30 and 250, with the CRCs verified. |
| Bzip2 Compress | redesigned | `bzip2:compress` | The bzip2 format written from its specification as Forge's own primitive (no library): Burrows-Wheeler transform by prefix doubling, move-to-front with zero runs, up to six Huffman tables with code lengths of at most 17, the bzip2 CRC-32. Block size (100s of kb) is block-size, 1 to 9, default 9 (else E_RANGE). Work factor is accepted (0 to 250, default 30, else E_RANGE) and ignored: it only tunes libbzip2's choice between two sorting algorithms, and Forge has one. The empty input gives the valid 14-byte empty stream instead of CyberChef's 'Please provide an input' error. The bytes can differ from libbzip2's (the Huffman refinement is not identical) except for tiny or very regular inputs, and bzip2, Python and libbzip2 read them. Cross-checked with CyberChef's libbzip2 (WebAssembly build) over 40 inputs of 0 bytes to 256 KiB: libbzip2 decompresses block sizes 1, 3 and 9 written here (also with its low-memory option), and 10 of 35 outputs (the small and regular inputs) equal libbzip2's byte for byte at block size 9. |
| Tar | redesigned | `tar:tar` | POSIX ustar in FL, one file as in CyberChef (filename, default file.txt). Header layout, mode default 0664 (436) and the empty owner names follow CyberChef; the data is padded to 512 bytes and two zero blocks end the archive. Added: mtime (Unix seconds, 0 by default so the output is the same on every run; CyberChef writes the current time), mode, uid and gid parameters. A name over 100 bytes is cut at a slash into the ustar prefix (up to 255 bytes in all, else E_RANGE; CyberChef overflows the field). GNU tar, bsdtar and Python read the output. Cross-checked (the clock fixed): the header and the padding equal CyberChef's except two fields: the user and group ids are seven octal digits here (CyberChef writes "0"), and the checksum is six digits, a NUL and a space as GNU tar writes it (CyberChef writes seven digits and a NUL, the sum over its own header). CyberChef's Untar reads the archives written here, and this reads CyberChef's. |
| Untar | redesigned | `tar:untar`, `tar:entry` | Returns a list of records (name, size, dir, mtime, mode, data) in archive order instead of CyberChef's list of files; mtime is Unix seconds and mode the permission bits. Files (types 0, NUL and 7) and directories (type 5) are listed, as in CyberChef; links, devices and FIFOs are skipped. Reads ustar (the prefix is joined to the name), v7 headers and the GNU long-name form (type L); PAX extended headers (x, g) are skipped and their path and size records are not applied. tar:entry (not a CyberChef row) takes one file's bytes by name. Added verify (on by default): each header's checksum must match, E_COERCE otherwise. Empty input, a bad octal field, or data that ends early is E_COERCE. An entry is a slice of the input, so the total never passes the input length. Cross-checked: reads every archive CyberChef's Tar writes, with the header checksums verified. |
| LZString Decompress | redesigned | `lzstring:decompress` | The same formats as Compress, and the same representation of the default format (an even number of bytes, E_COERCE otherwise). Empty input, a truncated stream (no end marker), a code naming no dictionary entry, a wrong alphabet and decompressed text that holds an unpaired surrogate are E_COERCE (the library returns null or an empty string for several of these). The format expands quadratically, so before the library runs a replay of the token structure with lengths only stops at the value limit with E_LIMIT_VALUE; a 4 MB bomb of a few KB is refused in milliseconds. The vectors come from the library itself: no independent implementation could be run locally. Cross-checked: decompresses CyberChef's output in all three formats. |
| LZString Compress | redesigned | `lzstring:compress` | lz-string 1.5.0 does the compressing. CyberChef's Compression Format (default, UTF16, Base64) is the format choice, with uri (compressToEncodedURIComponent) added. The result is bytes: Forge text cannot hold lone surrogates, which the default format's 16-bit units often contain (CyberChef shows that string as UTF-8, which cannot round-trip), so default is the units as UCS-2 big-endian byte pairs, exactly the library's compressToUint8Array; utf16 is compressToUTF16 written as UTF-8; base64 and uri are ASCII. The input is UTF-8 text (anything else is E_COERCE). The compressed values equal the library's. Cross-checked (the same lz-string library, 128 texts of 0 to 3,000 characters and one of 135,000, ASCII, Latin, Greek, CJK and control characters): all three of CyberChef's formats give the same 16-bit code units (default as big-endian byte pairs here, UTF16 and Base64 as the same text), and CyberChef decompresses them. |
| LZMA Decompress | covered | `lzma:decompress` | The .lzma format, with no options, as CyberChef's operation has none. Output is the same bytes CyberChef gives for a valid stream. The header is checked (a short header or a properties byte out of range is E_COERCE), and a declared size above the value limit is E_LIMIT_VALUE before anything is decoded. An unknown size (all 0xFF) is decoded only up to the limit: more output is E_LIMIT_VALUE, the decompression bomb rule of the wave 6 conventions. Truncated, corrupt data, and output whose length differs from the declared size, are E_COERCE. Cross-checked, see LZMA Compress. One CyberChef defect: its decompressor returns a JavaScript string for text and converts it back with Latin-1, so UTF-8 text whose characters are all at most U+00FF (an accented Latin text) comes back with each accent as a single byte, not as the UTF-8 sequence; this op returns the exact bytes. |
| LZMA Compress | redesigned | `lzma:compress` | The .lzma (LZMA alone) format over lzma1 0.6.1 (a port of XZ for Java), where CyberChef uses lzma-js. Compression Mode is the level parameter with the same 1 to 9 range and CyberChef's default of 7; there is no level 0, because the format has no store mode. The 13-byte header and the output are the same format, so xz --format=lzma, 7-Zip and Python's lzma module read the output, but the bytes differ from CyberChef's (a different encoder), and the outputs are pinned to lzma1 0.6.1. Out-of-range levels are E_RANGE. Cross-checked (40 inputs of 0 to 128 KiB, modes 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 against levels 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 and 9): CyberChef decompresses everything written here and this decompresses everything CyberChef writes. CyberChef's default is mode 7, the same as here. |
| LZ4 Decompress | redesigned | `lz4:decompress` | Frames (version, flags, block sizes; independent and linked blocks; stored blocks), with the header checksum, block checksums, content checksum and content size verified by default (verify; off recovers damaged data). Concatenated frames are joined, skippable frames are skipped and legacy frames (0x184C2102) are read; a dictionary id, an unknown magic number, trailing bytes that are not a frame (as the lz4 command rejects them) and cut-short data are E_COERCE. Output past the value limit is E_LIMIT_VALUE; the content size is never used to size a buffer. Raw (frameless) blocks, which CyberChef does not offer either, are not supported. Cross-checked: decompresses all 40 frames lz4js writes (0 to 256 KiB, six kinds of data) with the checksums verified. |
| LZ4 Compress | redesigned | `lz4:compress` | The LZ4 frame format written from the specification (no library; CyberChef uses lz4js, whose frame has independent 4 MB blocks and a content checksum, which are this op's defaults apart from level). Parameters added: level (0 stores, 1 to 9 a greedy hash-chain matcher following up to 2^(level-1) candidates; default 1), block-size (64KB to 4MB), independent, block-checksum, content-checksum and content-size. The bytes differ from lz4js and the lz4 command, but both read them (240 option combinations checked with lz4 v1.10.0 -d). Cross-checked with lz4js (the library CyberChef uses): lz4js decompresses the frames of every level 0 to 9, block size, independent or linked blocks, content checksum and content size setting (about 12,300 frames of 0 to 256 KiB). It does not read block checksums (its source has a TODO for them), so a frame with block-checksum on is read by the lz4 command, not by CyberChef. The default frame here (level 1, 4 MB blocks, content checksum) has the structure lz4js writes, but the compressed bytes differ. |
| LZNT1 Decompress | covered | `lznt1:decompress` | [MS-XCA] 2.5 (the Windows NTFS compression format, RtlDecompressBuffer), written from the specification; no parameters, as in CyberChef. The chunk loop is a private primitive (an FL prototype cost 12 to 49 VM steps per output byte). Added: corrupt data is E_COERCE naming the fault (bad chunk signature, a chunk or word cut short, a match before the start of its chunk, a chunk that expands past 4096 bytes), and output past the value limit stops with E_LIMIT_VALUE. A zero header ends the data and bytes after it are ignored; empty input is empty output. Compression is not offered (CyberChef has none). Cross-checked: the streams of the test encoder (with and without the end marker, stored and compressed chunks, 70 inputs of 0 to 256 KiB) decode the same here and in CyberChef, and 400 damaged streams (cut or with changed bytes) are rejected or decoded identically by both. Where they differ CyberChef is wrong: it takes a chunk header whose size field is 0 (a chunk of exactly one byte, which a 4097-byte input ends with) for the end marker and drops that chunk, while this treats only a zero header as the end. |
| XPRESS Decompress | covered | `xpress:decompress` | [MS-XCA] 2.3 and 2.4, Plain LZ77, written from the specification (the worked examples of section 3.1 are tests); no parameters. The decoder is a private primitive. Added: truncated data, a match before the start of the output and a bad long-length field are E_COERCE naming the fault, and output past the value limit stops with E_LIMIT_VALUE (a 32-bit match length allocates nothing). Empty input is E_COERCE because the stream starts with a flag word. Compression is not offered. Cross-checked: the streams of the test encoder (70 inputs of 0 to 256 KiB, including 32-bit match lengths) decode identically here and in CyberChef, and 400 damaged streams are rejected or decoded identically by both. |
| XPRESS LZ77+Huffman Decompress | covered | `xpress:huffman-decompress` | [MS-XCA] 2.1 and 2.2, LZ77+Huffman, written from the specification (the worked example of section 3.2 is a test); no parameters. The bit-level decoder is a private primitive. Blocks of 64 KiB follow one another, each with its own 256-byte table; the end-of-data symbol (256 with all input read) or a final 64 KiB block ends the data. Added: an over-subscribed or incomplete Huffman table, truncated data, a match before the start of the output and a bad long-length field are E_COERCE naming the fault, and output past the value limit stops with E_LIMIT_VALUE. Empty input is E_COERCE. Compression is not offered. Cross-checked: CyberChef takes the decompressed size as a parameter (4096 by default) and reads one block only; this finds the end itself and reads any number of 64 KiB blocks, each with its own table, as [MS-XCA] 2.2 describes (CyberChef fails on every stream of more than one block). For one block, CyberChef decodes most of the test encoder's streams but not all: it refills its bit buffer when fewer than 15 bits remain, this decoder when fewer than 16 remain (as the pseudo-code of the specification and Samba's lzxpress_huffman.c, read and not run), and the two read a following length byte from different places, so six of 57 single-block streams fail in CyberChef (match offset out of range or truncated bit stream). The symbol 256 ends the data here when all input has been read, CyberChef ends when the declared size is reached; a stream whose last symbols hold a real match of length 3 at distance 1 (also symbol 256) in the final 32 bits is therefore read short here, a case the test encoder avoids and no Windows encoder is known to produce. Bytes after the last block are E_COERCE here (no size to stop at), ignored by CyberChef. |

## Hashing (48)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Analyse hash | covered | `hash-analysis:analyse` | Takes hex text and returns a text report: length in hex characters, bytes and bits, and the hashing functions whose digest has that size (every size CyberChef names, down to the 4-bit checksums, so an odd number of hex digits is accepted). The table is Forge's own and lists some functions that Forge has not implemented. Text that is not hex is an error. |
| Generate all checksums | redesigned | `generate-all:checksums` | A text report, one checksum per line with its hex: the 171 CRC presets, Adler-32 and Fletcher-8, -16, -32 and -64, with the same Length and Include names parameters. The CRCs are computed by one private primitive that shares the loop of crc:_crc and that the tests hold equal to crc:checksum; the order of the lines is the CRC table first, then the other checksums. |
| Generate all hashes | redesigned | `generate-all:hashes` | A text report, one hash per line with its hex, built from the digest words: MD2 to MD6, SHA-0 to SHA-3, Keccak, SHAKE, RIPEMD, HAS-160, Whirlpool, BLAKE2, BLAKE3, Streebog, GOST, Snefru, SM3, the LM hash, the NT hash and SSDEEP, with the same Length and Include names parameters. The LM hash line sits where CyberChef has it, just before the NT hash; like the NT hash it reads the input as UTF-8 text and shows a note on its line (the report still completes) for input that is not text it can take (the LM hash takes characters up to U+00FF only). Not included: Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T, and the CTPH line (see CTPH). Lines CyberChef does not have: SHA-512/224 and /256, BLAKE3 and Snefru. |
| MD2 | covered | `md2:digest` | Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Only the standard 18 rounds of RFC 1319 exist; CyberChef's Rounds parameter is not supported. |
| MD4 | covered | `md4:digest` | RFC 1320. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| MD5 | covered | `md5:digest` | No parameters. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| MD6 | covered | `md6:digest` | Parameters size (bits, a multiple of 8, 8 to 512, default 256), levels (L, 0 to 64, default 64) and key (up to 64 bytes), with CyberChef's defaults. Sizes that are not a multiple of 8 bits are not supported. The round count is the report's default (40 + size/4, at least 80 with a key). |
| SHA0 | covered | `sha0:digest` | FIPS 180 (1993). Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Only the standard 80 rounds exist; a Rounds parameter is not supported. |
| SHA1 | covered | `sha1:digest` | No parameters. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| SHA2 | covered | `sha2:digest` | One word with a size parameter: 224, 256, 384, 512 (the default, as in CyberChef), 512/224, 512/256. Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). CyberChef's Rounds parameter is not supported: only the FIPS 180-4 round counts exist. |
| SHA3 | covered | `sha3:digest` | One word with a size parameter in bits: 224, 256, 384, 512 (the default, as in CyberChef). Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| SM3 | covered | `sm3:digest` | Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). CyberChef's Length and Rounds parameters are not supported: the standard GB/T 32905-2016 has one 256-bit output and 64 rounds. |
| Keccak | covered | `keccak:digest` | One word with a size parameter in bits: 224, 256, 384, 512 (the default, as in CyberChef), with the original Keccak padding (not SHA-3). |
| Shake | redesigned | `shake:digest` | The output length is in bytes (1 to 65536, default 64), where CyberChef's Size is in bits (default 512, so the default is the same 64 bytes; the bits are a multiple of 8 in Forge). The variant is 128 or 256, the security strength in bits, as in CyberChef's Capacity (default 256 in both). |
| RIPEMD | covered | `ripemd:digest` | One word with a size choice of 128, 160, 256 or 320 (default 320, as in CyberChef). Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). ripemd160:digest also exists, for HMAC. |
| HAS-160 | covered | `has160:digest` | Returns raw bytes (chain hex:encode). CyberChef's Rounds parameter is not supported: only the standard 80 steps exist. |
| Whirlpool | covered | `whirlpool:digest` | The final ISO/IEC 10118-3 version, raw bytes (chain hex:encode). The Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T variants and the Rounds parameter are not offered: the variants have no citable vectors in the original papers, and Whirlpool-0 has a different, random S-box. Only the standard 10 rounds exist. |
| Snefru | covered | `snefru:digest` | Size 128 or 256 (default 128) and Rounds 2, 4 or 8 (default 8), as in CyberChef; CyberChef also accepts other sizes in steps of 32 bits up to 480, which the Snefru reference does not define. Raw bytes (chain hex:encode). Implemented from Merkle's Xerox reference distribution 2.5a, whose S-boxes it uses. |
| BLAKE2b | redesigned | `blake2b:digest` | The output size is in bytes (16, 20, 32, 48 or 64, default 64), where CyberChef's Size is in bits (128, 160, 256, 384, 512, default 512). The key is an optional key of up to 64 bytes in any of the key encodings. |
| BLAKE2s | redesigned | `blake2s:digest` | The output size is in bytes (16, 20 or 32, default 32), where CyberChef's Size is in bits (128, 160, 256, default 256). The key is an optional key of up to 32 bytes in any of the key encodings. |
| BLAKE3 | covered | `blake3:digest` | The output length is in bytes (1 to 65536, default 32, the BLAKE3 specification's default output; CyberChef's default is 16). The key is an optional 32-byte key, as in CyberChef. |
| Ascon Hash | covered | `ascon:hash` | Ascon-Hash256 of NIST SP 800-232, the only variant CyberChef offers. The output is the 32 raw bytes (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's hex text). |
| Ascon MAC | redesigned | `ascon:mac` | Ascon-Mac with a 16-byte key param (E_RANGE otherwise) and a 16-byte tag, as CyberChef. It is the PRF-based MAC of the Ascon designers' reference code (ascon-c, the asconmacv13 known answers), which CyberChef labels with SP 800-232 although that standard does not define a MAC. The output is raw bytes (chain hex:encode for hex text). |
| GOST Hash | covered | `gost:digest`, `streebog:digest` | GOST R 34.11-94 is gost:digest with an sbox parameter: test (RFC 5831, CyberChef's D-TEST) or cryptopro (RFC 4357, CyberChef's D-A, the default here and the one its Generate all hashes uses). CyberChef's own default, E-TEST, and its other E-* sets are the sets of the 28147-89 cipher, not hash parameter sets, and are not offered. GOST R 34.11-2012 is the separate streebog:digest. Only the test and CryptoPro hash S-box sets are offered. Raw bytes (chain hex:encode). |
| Streebog | covered | `streebog:digest` | Size 256 or 512, as in CyberChef. Raw bytes (chain hex:encode), in the byte order of the RFC 6986 examples reversed (little-endian), which is the conventional digest string. |
| SSDEEP | covered | `ssdeep:digest` | Context triggered piecewise hashing (Kornblum 2006) as the reference ssdeep program computes it. The result is text, blocksize:hash1:hash2, not bytes: it is a structured string that the compare word reads piece by piece. |
| CTPH | redesigned | `ssdeep:ctph` | CyberChef's CTPH is a second implementation of the same idea whose text differs from its own SSDEEP (the block size is written in another form and the pieces differ), and its algorithm is not documented beyond that library. Forge has one fuzzy hash, the reference ssdeep one, and ctph is an alias of ssdeep:digest under the name of the 2006 paper; the text is not CyberChef's CTPH text. |
| Compare SSDEEP hashes | covered | `ssdeep:compare` | The 0 to 100 score of the reference algorithm: block size check, runs of more than three equal characters cut to three, a common substring of 7 characters, a weighted edit distance (insert and remove 1, replace 2) and the cap for small block sizes. The first hash is the data input and the second is the other parameter. Text that is not an ssdeep hash is an error here, where CyberChef scores it 0. |
| Compare CTPH hashes | redesigned | `ssdeep:compare-ctph` | CyberChef's Compare CTPH hashes reads its own CTPH text, which Forge does not produce (see CTPH). compare-ctph is an alias of ssdeep:compare and scores ssdeep text. |
| HMAC | covered | `hmac:digest` | Hash choice: md2, md4, md5, sha0, sha1, sha224, sha256 (the default; CyberChef's first choice, and so its default, is MD2), sha384, sha512, sha512/224, sha512/256, ripemd128, ripemd160, ripemd256, ripemd320, has160, whirlpool and snefru, which are every CyberChef choice except Whirlpool-0 and Whirlpool-T (Forge does not implement those variants of Whirlpool). The four SHA-3 sizes (sha3-224, sha3-256, sha3-384, sha3-512) are extra: CyberChef's HMAC has no SHA-3. snefru is Snefru with a 128-bit output and 8 passes, as CyberChef uses. The key is a key param in any of the key encodings (utf8, hex, latin1 or base64; CyberChef also offers Decimal, which Forge does not), empty by default. The output is the raw MAC bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. Blake2 and BLAKE3 keyed modes are their own words. |
| CMAC | redesigned | `cmac:digest` | NIST SP 800-38B and RFC 4493. The input is the message, the key is a key param (hex, utf8, latin1 or base64) and the algorithm is AES (default) or TDES (CyberChef's Triple DES). AES takes 16, 24 or 32 bytes, Triple DES 16 (two-key, K3 = K1) or 24 bytes, and another length is E_RANGE. The output is the raw tag, 16 bytes for AES and 8 for Triple DES (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's hex text). The block cipher is a private primitive that calls the TypeScript AES and Triple DES block functions directly, because the block words of those vocabularies are private. |
| Bcrypt compare | redesigned | `bcrypt:compare` | The input is the password and the hash is a str param. The result is a bool, where CyberChef returns the text Match: <password> or No match. A string that is not a well-formed bcrypt hash (2a, 2b or 2y, a cost of 04 to 31, 22 salt and 31 hash characters) is E_COERCE, where CyberChef raises an error; a cost in it above 16 is E_RANGE. The comparison is constant time. |
| Bcrypt parse | covered | `bcrypt:parse` | The input is the hash text. The report has CyberChef's four lines: Rounds, Salt (prefix, cost and the 22 salt characters), Password hash and Full hash. A string that is not a well-formed bcrypt hash is E_COERCE. Parsing does no hashing, so any cost from 04 to 31 is reported. |
| Argon2 | redesigned | `argon2:derive` | The input is the password. Salt (default the text somesalt), iterations (3), memory in KiB (4096), parallelism (1), hash length in bytes (32) and type (argon2i, argon2d or argon2id; default argon2i) are CyberChef's. The output is a choice of encoded (the PHC string $argon2i$v=19$m=4096,t=3,p=1$salt$hash, as ASCII bytes; the default, as CyberChef) or raw hash bytes; CyberChef's Hex hash is raw chained through hex:encode. The salt must be at least 8 bytes. Limits (E_RANGE): memory 8 to 262,144 KiB (256 MiB), iterations 1 to 64, memory times iterations at most 1,048,576 (about 2.5 s), parallelism 1 to 64, length 4 to 1024; the defaults take about 40 ms. |
| Argon2 compare | redesigned | `argon2:compare` | The input is the password and the encoded hash is a str param. The result is a bool, where CyberChef returns the text Match: <password> or No match. A string that is not a well-formed encoded Argon2 hash (type, optional version, m, t and p, unpadded base64 salt of at least 8 bytes and hash of at least 4) is E_COERCE, where CyberChef reports No match; the cost in the string is held to the limits of argon2:derive (E_RANGE). The comparison is constant time. |
| NT Hash | covered | `nthash:digest` | MD4 of the UTF-16LE text (MS-NLMP NTOWFv1), 16 raw bytes. Takes text, not bytes. |
| LM Hash | redesigned | `lmhash:digest` | The password is the input text, upper-cased and then cut at 14 bytes, as CyberChef does (so a character that upper-cases to two, such as the German sharp s, counts twice). It is encoded as ISO 8859-1 where CyberChef's library writes the low byte of each character. The output is the 16 raw bytes (chain hex:encode for CyberChef's hex text). A character above U+00FF cannot be written in ISO 8859-1 and is E_COERCE, where CyberChef's library keeps its low byte. |
| MurmurHash3 | covered | `murmur3:digest` | MurmurHash3 x86_32 with a 32-bit seed (default 0), written in FL; CyberChef offers only this 32-bit variant too, and the x86_128 and x64_128 variants are not implemented here either. Returns the 32-bit value as 4 raw bytes in big-endian order, the usual hex form (chain hex:encode); CyberChef shows the same value as an unsigned decimal (or signed, with its option). Forge hashes the bytes of the input; CyberChef hashes the low 8 bits of each character, so the two agree for byte-valued text and differ for text beyond Latin-1. |
| Fletcher-8 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 8. The output is 1 raw byte (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Fletcher-16 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 16. The output is 2 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Fletcher-32 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 32. The output is 4 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Fletcher-64 Checksum | covered | `fletcher:checksum` | size 64. The output is 8 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Adler-32 Checksum | covered | `adler32:checksum` | The output is 4 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. |
| Luhn Checksum | redesigned | `luhn:check-digit`, `luhn:validate` | Two words, the check digit and a validity flag, instead of a three-line report whose "validated string" is not a validation. The radix is a parameter in both (an even number from 2 to 36, default 10). CyberChef's "Checksum" line, the sum modulo the radix of the input as given, is not offered on its own: validate is true when that sum is 0. The check digit is one lowercase character, as in CyberChef. The empty input gives the empty check digit in both; validate is false for it. |
| CRC Checksum | covered | `crc:checksum`, `crc:custom` | Presets by CyberChef's names (all 171, with the same parameters); custom parameters in crc:custom. The output is raw bytes (ceil(width/8) of them), not hex text padded to ceil(width/4) digits. The default is the CRC-32 preset (CyberChef's default is Custom, with width 0), and crc:custom defaults to the CRC-32 parameters (CyberChef's are all 0) and accepts widths of 1 to 82 bits. |
| TCP/IP Checksum | covered | `tcpip:checksum` | Folds the carry until it is gone (RFC 1071), while CyberChef folds it once, so for some inputs (for example the bytes ff ff ff ff 00 01) CyberChef prints "-1" where RFC 1071 gives fffe. The output is 2 raw bytes (chain hex:encode), always four hex digits; CyberChef shows hex text without padding to four digits (0x0f67 shows as "f67"). Confirmed in CyberChef's TCPIPChecksum.mjs: one fold, then Utils.hex(0xffff - csum) with the default padding of 2. |
| XOR Checksum | covered | `xor-checksum:checksum` | The default blocksize is 4, the same as CyberChef's. The output is blocksize raw bytes (chain hex:encode), where CyberChef shows hex text. A short last block is treated as zero-padded in both. The blocksize is 1 to 65536 in Forge; CyberChef accepts any positive integer. |
| Parity Bit | covered | `parity:encode`, `parity:decode` | Two words, encode and decode, instead of an Encode/Decode switch. parity:decode verifies the parity by default (verify=true) and raises E_COERCE on a mismatch or an unexpected character, whereas CyberChef's decode strips the bit without checking; verify=false gives CyberChef's behaviour. The one exception is an empty block between delimiters, for which decode raises E_COERCE ("no parity bit to remove") even with verify=false, where CyberChef returns the empty block. The default position is end, where CyberChef's first (default) Position is Start; the default mode is even in both. Encoding is the same. |

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |

| Detect File Type | redesigned | `filetype:detect` | A table of about 150 signatures (name, extensions, MIME type, description, magic bytes with offsets and masks) in src/filetype-sigs.ts, written from the format documents and file(1)'s magic list, not copied from CyberChef: images, video, audio, documents (PDF, RTF, OLE2, OOXML and ODF by their first ZIP entry, EPUB), applications (ELF, PE and DOS MZ told apart by the PE header, Mach-O, Java class, DEX, WebAssembly), archives (ZIP, JAR, RAR 4 and 5, 7z, gzip, bzip2, xz, Zstandard, tar, cab, cpio, ar, RPM, ISO, ...) and miscellaneous (SQLite, pcap and pcapng, bplist, DER certificates, PEM, LNK, fonts, registry hives). The seven category switches are CyberChef's. Output is File type, Extension, MIME type and Description for every match at offset 0, a blank line between matches, and CyberChef's text for no match, and a blank line between matches; the names and extensions are Forge's own table, so they differ from CyberChef's in places (an APK or a JAR is a ZIP whose first entry says so, or just a ZIP). Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read: the four lines (File type:, Extension:, MIME type: with three spaces and Description:, the last only when the description is not empty), the blank line between matches and the text for no match are CyberChef's. |
| Scan for Embedded Files | redesigned | `filetype:scan` | Every offset of the data where a signature of the same table matches (the file would start there; a signature at an offset such as tar's ustar at 257 is reported at the start of the file), ordered by offset, as text in CyberChef's layout: its introductory sentence, then Offset N (0xN): and the four indented lines of Detect File Type for each match, or No embedded files were found. (no total line). The category switches are CyberChef's (Miscellaneous off by default). Added parameter ignore-common (default on; CyberChef 11.5.0 has no such option and reports every match): it leaves out the short signatures that occur by chance in any data (MZ, ICO and CUR, MPEG audio and AAC frame sync, a shebang, zlib headers, ...). The scan is one primitive (filetype:scan-list, public so that the YARA ops reuse it): 5 ms for 64 KiB and one VM step; the report is FL. More matches than the value limit allows is E_LIMIT_VALUE. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read; the signature table is Forge's own, so the matches differ in places. |
| YARA Rules | redesigned | `yara:scan` | CyberChef runs libyara compiled to WebAssembly; Forge has no WASM, so the rules run on a documented subset of YARA 4 written for Forge (rule parser, string matchers and condition evaluator in TypeScript behind one private primitive, regular expressions only through the regex seam, so an untrusted recipe needs the hard kill). Supported: rule names, tags, private and global rules, meta (string, integer, boolean); text strings with ascii, wide, nocase, fullword, xor (with a range), base64 and base64wide (with an alphabet); hex strings with wildcards, nibble wildcards, ~, jumps and nested alternatives; regular expressions (classes, groups, alternation, greedy and lazy quantifiers, anchors, \b; no back references or look-around); and conditions with boolean operators, filesize, $a, #a, @a[i], !a[i], at, in, N of / any of / all of / none of / N% of with sets, for ... of and for ... in loops, int8 to uint32 reads (little and big endian), 64-bit integer arithmetic and references to earlier rules. Anything else is E_COERCE with the line and column: modules (the message names pe, elf, math, hash, ...), include, entrypoint, floating point numbers, string operators, defined, uint64, wide or xor on a regular expression. Limits: 100,000 matches per string (libyara 1,000,000), 4 MiB of input, 200 million byte steps (E_LIMIT_VALUE). The matches agree with libyara 4.5.4 (473 cases from yara-python, 366 of them random), except for hex alternatives of different length that start alike, where libyara sometimes reports the shorter path (Forge takes the first choice that lets the rest match), and Latin-1 case folding for /i on regular expressions. Output in CyberChef's layout: a rule with no string match, or with Show strings and Show string lengths both off, is Input matches rule "name" [metadata] (N times). and otherwise Rule "name" [metadata] matches (N times): followed by one line Pos n, [length n, ]identifier $a[, data: "..."] per match, the strings in order; N is the number of matches of all the strings of the rule and is shown with Show counts, which is on by default as CyberChef's; no matching rule gives empty text. Parameters in CyberChef's order: Rules, Show strings, Show string lengths, Show metadata, Show counts; CyberChef's Show rule warnings and Show console module messages are not provided (no modules, no warnings). Differences kept: the data of a match is escaped and cut at 32 bytes (CyberChef prints it raw), CyberChef writes two spaces before the count of the short form ("name"  (4 times).) and Forge one, and CyberChef puts libyara's compile errors in the output while Forge raises E_COERCE. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source and its tests read (libyara compiled to WebAssembly was not run). |

| ELF Info | redesigned | `elf:info` | The layout and the values of `readelf -W -h -l -S -s` for ELF32 and ELF64, little and big endian, checked block for block against GNU readelf 2.42 on real and hand-built files (executables, shared objects, ELF32 BE MIPS, ARM, PowerPC64, RISC-V, GNU and FreeBSD OS/ABIs): the header, the program headers (with the interpreter line and DYN (Position-Independent Executable file) from DT_FLAGS_1), the section headers with their names, and .symtab and .dynsym with value, size, type, bind, visibility, section index and name. At most 2,000 rows a table, then a line with the number of the others. The names of the 213 machines, the OS/ABIs, section types and segment types are readelf's. Not shown: machine-specific flag words in the header Flags field, machine-specific section and segment type names (ARM EXIDX, MIPS RTPROC), the 'Section to Segment mapping', symbol versions and the dynamic section. Data that is not ELF, a table that runs past the data, or counts and offsets that lie are E_COERCE with the offset. CyberChef's own report is not readelf's: Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source and its tests read; it prints '= ELF Header =' blocks of 'Label:' lines padded to 30 characters (decimal addresses, binary flags, a section name per section, the names of the symbols only) and has defects (the .strtab case falls through to .symtab, so symbol names are read from the wrong table; no symbol values, types or bindings; the program header flags are in a different position for 32 and 64 bits). Forge keeps the readelf layout, which carries all of that information, as a deliberate difference; it is a layout the owner may still want changed. |

| Generate De Bruijn Sequence | covered | `de-bruijn:generate` | The lexicographically least de Bruijn sequence B(k, n), the same as CyberChef's for the alphabets it has (k 2 to 9, written 0 to 8; n from 2). Forge reaches further: k up to 36 (digits then letters), n from 1 to 16, k to the power n at most 65,536 symbols (CyberChef 50,000). The input is ignored. |
| Generate UUID | covered | `uuid:generate` | One parameterised word for RFC 9562: v1, v3, v4 (the CyberChef default), v5, v6, v7, nil and max, as lower-case 8-4-4-4-12 text. v3 and v5 take a namespace (any UUID, CyberChef's default 1b671a64-40d5-491e-99b0-da01ff1f3341 if none is given, or dns, url, oid, x500) and a name, which is the input when the name parameter is empty as in CyberChef; they are deterministic and equal CyberChef's. v1 and v6 count 100 ns ticks but the host clock has millisecond resolution, so the finer digits are zero; the clock sequence and the node are random (node with the multicast bit set). |
| Analyse UUID | redesigned | `uuid:analyse` | Reads a UUID (hyphens, braces, a urn:uuid: prefix and either case are accepted) and reports, one per line, the version and what it means, the variant and, for versions 1, 6 and 7, the timestamp in UTC (with the 100 ns digits of versions 1 and 6); nil and max UUIDs are named. The wording and the layout are Forge's own: CyberChef writes labelled blocks (Version:, Timestamp:, Timestamp (ISO):, Node:, Clock:, UUID Integer:) and only for versions 1, 6 and 7. Text that is not 32 hex digits is E_COERCE. |
| Generate TOTP | covered | `otp:totp` | RFC 6238 over hmac:digest. The input is the Base32 secret as authenticator apps show it; an empty input makes a random secret of key-size bytes (20 by default, as CyberChef). The result is CyberChef's two parts, URI: <otpauth URI>, a blank line, Password: <digits>, and the passwords equal CyberChef's for the same secret and time. Name (Account), code length (digits, 6) and interval (period, 30) follow CyberChef's options; additions are the HMAC hash (sha1 by default, also sha256 and sha512) and an explicit Unix time (-1, the default, is now) so the vectors of RFC 6238 appendix B can be reproduced. The epoch offset (T0) is applied as RFC 6238 says; CyberChef ignores it. |
| Generate HOTP | covered | `otp:hotp` | RFC 4226 over hmac:digest, with the same input, output and options as otp:totp except that the counter replaces the time (counter 0 by default, up to 2^64 - 1). Matches the values of RFC 4226 appendix D and CyberChef's output. |
| Generate QR Code | redesigned | `qr:generate` | A QR Code Model 2 encoder written from ISO/IEC 18004 (numeric, alphanumeric and byte mode chosen for the whole text, versions 1 to 40, error correction L, M, Q and H, Reed-Solomon, the eight masks with the penalty rules of 7.8.3; the module matrix equals python-qrcode's for the 233 inputs tried) with the writers in primitives and the PNG file in FL over the deflate and crc words. Formats: svg (the default here; CyberChef's default is PNG, but the output pane shows no images and an SVG is text), text (two characters a module) and a 1-bit PNG. Parameters in CyberChef's order: format, module size (default 5), margin in modules (default 4), error correction (default M; the choices are L, M, Q, H for Low, Medium, Quartile, High). Not provided: JPEG, EPS and PDF output (no image library is in scope; JPEG is not a sensible format for a QR code), kanji mode and ECI headers (UTF-8 bytes are written without an ECI header, as most generators do), Micro QR and mixed-mode segments (one mode for the whole text, so the code can be larger than a mixed-mode encoder's). Empty text, text that does not fit version 40 and parameters out of range are E_RANGE. Vectors from python-qrcode (single mode, auto version and mask), the ISO example codewords, and the PNG decoded with Pillow and the host's zlib. Checked against CyberChef 11.5.0 (WP 5.59c): the source read (it uses qr-image and Jimp); CyberChef's own output was not compared bit for bit, the module matrix is the standard's. |
| Parse QR Code | not yet |  |  |
| Haversine distance | covered | `coords:haversine` | The input is CyberChef's one line, lat1, lng1, lat2, lng2 in decimal degrees, or the two positions on two lines, each in any format that Convert co-ordinate format reads; the radius is a number in kilometres (6371 by default); the result is in metres, rounded to the millimetre, as decimal text (CyberChef prints the full floating-point number, the same to the millimetre). |
| HTML To Text | redesigned | `html-text:to-text` | CyberChef's operation only turns an HTML-typed output into text (on text it returns its input unchanged). Forge has no typed outputs, so the word reads HTML source instead: comments, script and style elements, the DOCTYPE and all tags are dropped (br and block-level tags become line feeds), character references are decoded with html:decode, runs of line feeds are cut to two and the text is trimmed. It is a pattern-based stripper, not a parser, and not a sanitiser. |
| Generate Lorem Ipsum | redesigned | `lorem:generate` | Paragraphs (up to 500), sentences (up to 5,000), words or bytes (up to 65,536), chosen at random from Forge's own list of the 182 distinct words of two passages of Cicero's De finibus (public domain), starting with the traditional Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetur adipiscing elit. unless opening is off. The sentence and paragraph shapes are Forge's own; CyberChef's word list, its closing full stop on a run of words and its sentence lengths are not copied. The input is ignored. |
| Numberwang | dropped |  | A joke based on a comedy sketch; it has no data-processing use. |
| XKCD Random Number | dropped |  | A joke: it always returns 4 (the xkcd 'random number'). |
| Automated Validation Test Op | dropped |  | CyberChef's internal fixture for testing parameter validation; it is not a user operation. |

## Flow control (10)

| CyberChef | Status | Forge | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Magic | not yet |  |  |
| Fork | redesigned | `step:fork` | A structural fork step (RECIPES section 3.2) holds its child steps; split and join are part of the step. |
| Subsection | redesigned | `step:subsection` | A structural step that runs its children on each regex match and leaves the rest of the data alone. |
| Merge | redesigned | `step:fork` | No separate step: a fork step joins its pieces when its children end. |
| Register | not yet |  |  |
| Label | redesigned | `step:repeat` | Loops are structural repeat steps (a count or until stable), not labels. |
| Jump | redesigned | `step:repeat` | Loops are structural repeat steps (a count or until stable), not jumps. |
| Conditional Jump | redesigned | `step:if` | Branching is a tree: an if step holds then and else steps, so there are no labels or jumps. |
| Return | not yet |  |  |
| Comment | redesigned | `step:comment` | A structural comment step with no effect on the data. |
